Binary matrices that constantly margin are used extensively across various scientific and engineering disciplines to create two-level designs with orthogonal row and column sums. Previous research primarily relied on uniform sampling methods, which presents significant storage and computational challenges. This paper introduces an innovative non-uniform sampling approach to select these matrices, accompanied by theoretical proofs demonstrating its efficacy. The proposed method's advantages lie in its efficient storage and rapid generation of constant margin binary matrices. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to the generation of new and existing designs, including Kharaghani-Lawrence-Massey arrays and those based on relative difference zones. The sampling technique also successfully recovers existing construction methods, offering a novel way to sample constant margin binary matrices.

Predictive power of the Standard Model is constrained by parton distribution functions (PDFs), which are measured through various experiments and vary depending on the PDF set being used. To tackle the growing uncertainties in PDFs, a new framework is proposed that allows for fine-tuning of PDFs to enhance their predictive accuracy for processes not included in the PDF fitting procedure. The proposed framework exponentiates non-perturbative matrix elements of local twist-2 operators that are Hermitian and conserved. By treating these matrix elements as variational parameters, they can be precisely adjusted to improve predictions for specific LHC processes. Building upon the standard PDF framework, this new adjustment method leverages analytical properties of PDFs and the evolution equations of DGLAP to maintain consistency without compromising the predictive value of PDFs. The approach primarily targets modifications to PDFs at low values of x and low x-x bar x, making it particularly suitable for addressing predictions related to small-x phenomena and high-luminage Higgs measurements at the HL-LHC.

This paper highlights the strengths of the heaviest data mining library in terms of codebase size, focusing on its latest release 0.7.5 'Heidelberg'. Also known as ELKI, this open-source library offers a comprehensive collection of tools to facilitate various data mining processes. It includes efficient implementations of numerous algorithms along with functionalities to support data set generation, indexing, and performance comparison through micro- and macro-scoping approaches. Its modular architecture enables adaptation to computer systems of varying scales, from personal computers to high-performance computing setups. In addition to its core library, related software collections such as an artificial neural network library and a statistical computation package are explored. All these toolsets are unified by their commitment to permissive open-source licenses and thorough unit testing protocols.

A new technique has been developed to rapidly create optical frequency grids by detecting resonances in an accelerated microresonator while changing its tuning rate. This method, which uses a simple detector, can produce grid outcomes comparable to those achieved by more complex feedback methods, but with the added benefit of being able to identify new resonances as they emerge. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique by successfully creating and locking a grid of 500 lasers.

We establish a classification system for a specific type of dipolar action known as acylindrically hyperbolic group actions. Dipolar actions, which are collections of pairwise non-preserving axial lines, are complemented by a series of preserved subgroups, which we explore. We demonstrate that faithful invariant stochastic subgroups within these groups generate either cyclic or finitely generated random subgroups. Furthermore, we explore the implications of faithful invariant stochastic subgroups in acylindrically hyperbolic group actions, demonstrating that such subgroups must generate the entire group if not cyclic. Additionally, a detailed examination will be provided, focusing on examples that showcase both loyal and unfaithful invariant stochastic subgroups in acylindrically hyperbolic group actions.

Quantization is an effective model compression technique, but its impact on model generalization remains unclear.
This anomaly can be attributed to a lack of theoretical understanding about how binary neural networks operate.
By examining the neural tangent space, we were able to derive explicit formulas for the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions,
which illuminate the characteristics of binary networks during the training process.
Furthermore, we were able to show that on regression tasks, certain spectral regions contribute negatively to the generalization error.
By contrast, these same spectral regions yield positive generalization errors when activation functions are real-valued.
Through numerical experiments, we validated the superiority of binary weights in terms of generalization performance.

In this research, we employ a specific entropy structure to derive extreme surfaces in quantum systems. Extending the concept of extreme surfaces beyond 1/dimensionality, we find that these surfaces mark a transition in entropy scaling from area to volume law as demonstrated with a 3/dimensional tensor network state. Additionally, applying a gradient of entropy considerations leads to an optimal entropy profile and, consequently, extreme surfaces in varied holographic models including bulk black holes with their own horizons beyond the extreme surface location. Furthermore, we explore the connection between extreme surfaces and entanglement entropy, revealing that they correspond to the minimal surface in the bulk as proposed by Ryu-Takayanagi. However, in cases involving bulk black holes, there's competition between the extreme surface and the holographic horizon due to their respective expansions, resulting in the dominance of one over the other.

We introduce a new category multiplier applicable to resolvable lattice models 
of combinatorial objects, determining that the number of grid elements 
intersecting lines of various colors is equivalent to the product of numbers 
associated with each color. This multiplier has practical use in constructing 
resolvable designs. Furthermore, a generalized form of the multiplier is 
described.

This paper focuses on resolving non-linear, convex optimization issues related to compressed sensing through the use of convex iteratives and acceleration techniques. Several acceleration methods for compressed sensing, solved via convex optimization, are analyzed within the framework of Hilbert space operators. These analytical evaluations lead to the discovery of general stabilization techniques that can be applied to this class of algorithms. The effectiveness of these stabilization methods is demonstrated using empirical results from compressed sensing applications.

We examine the characteristics of combined images formed by merging multiple images and their respective weights. These form a linear combination that can be analyzed using the effective point spread function (PSF), which we investigate by employing the effective covariance matrix approach. This analysis provides insight into the effective PSF governing second-order correlations in such combined images. Notably, we demonstrate that the effective PSF does not merely reflect the median PSFs across all input images; rather it depends on the correlation matrix of the input images' fluctuations. We use effective PSFs to define novel notions of effective full width at half maximum and effective eccentricity for characterizing the blur shape in characterizing blur. These concepts are illustrated using numerical examples, such as combining images of varying telescope beam sizes or stack of weighted spectra with varied spectral instrument resolution.

We introduce new probabilistic models for Gaussian free fields in two-dimensional domains, related to systems of multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution evolution paths driven by log-gas random variables, covering both fixed-coupling and strobe models. These field models satisfy the Dirichlet boundary condition and exhibit connection to Brownian loop soups in a given domain.

For three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with periodic boundary conditions, we establish an existence theory and find the precise limit of the initial boundary period relative to the viscosity coefficient, beyond which smooth solutions cease to be guaranteed and multiple solutions may arise even for single, smooth, and periodically bounded initial conditions. Our findings are analogous to the a priori extremal theory but apply specifically to periodic starting data and yield an exact threshold of the Bourier number. Additionally, we demonstrate the formation of high-energy, turbulent, and potentially non-smooth solutions beyond this threshold, and explore various scenarios of solution non-uniqueness.

This research proposes an innovative, linear-time validation method for assessing the norm distance between quantum states, utilizing classical computation. Building on earlier work by specific authors, this method's approach has been refined and optimized for efficiency. First, we introduce a novel technique for calculating the squared norm distance, resulting in a time complexity of O(n log n) and a significance factor of n. Subsequently, we refine this approach, developing a validated algorithm runtime of O(n log log n) with the assistance of precomputation.

Generating diverse cell shapes that adhere to specified constraints poses a complex challenge, particularly when input data consists of shape descriptions like Euler characteristics instead of direct spatial information. This challenge has significant ramifications, as it enables the creation of cells that can be physically created through 3D printing techniques, thus facilitating studies on cell function-related shape restrictions. To address this, we've developed a generation network that utilizes implicit neural representation, leveraging available cell shape data to produce implicit models of cells matching specified constraints, and further guides these shapes through 曼德博转换 to optimize their morphology. Our approach has been successfully tested on two biological systems exhibiting diverse shape variations, demonstrating the creation of high-quality cell shapes that maintain the original dataset's distribution patterns, and also allows for the shape customization of these cells.

Inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate an unconditioned reinforcement problem to model spatial representations in hippocampal thalamocortical circuits, mimicking their response patterns to an agent's movements in 3D space. Our spiking neural network, trained solely on temporal artifact spikes, reproduces a thalamocortical hippocampal system, and we demonstrate that place cells can spontaneously develop stable, 2D-like representations of a 3D environment. Furthermore, we reveal that the cross-product matrix of input signals can and should be utilized to induce stable depictions of high-dimensional environments in neural networks, and we reveal various topological transformations that utilize the cross-product matrix to induce representations of complex spaces.

Expanding on earlier simulations by Molin and Maggs of 2D hard-disk magnets, 
we found that both the ferromagnetic and anti-ferromagnetic types exhibit irreversibility.
However, the degree of anti-ferromagnetic irrevisibility significantly surpasses that of the ferromagnetic type.
Interestingly, our results reveal that systems with even numbers of anti-ferromagnetic particles display fewer signs of irrevisibility compared to those with odd numbers,
indicating an alternating pattern of irrevisibility depth as particle numbers change.

The challenge of localizing sound sources involves determining the precise origin point of acoustic sources in a three-dimensional space. However, accurately detecting and localizing all sound sources can be a challenging task due to several complex factors, including occlusion, absorption, non-stationarity, and cross-channel interference. These challenges are further compounded by the need to distinguish and identify each sound event, which can be a difficult task for both humans and automated systems. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a machine learning-based approach that utilizes fully-convolutional neural networks to simultaneously detect, localize, and identify sound sources. To improve accuracy and robustness, we have implemented advanced data enhancement techniques that rotate microphones and apply frequency rectangular filters to the raw data. This method is highly efficient and can be easily integrated with existing deep learning architectures without the need for microphone-matrix-matching. As such, it serves as a valuable pre-processing step that increases system robustness to real-world occlusion and absorption challenges. Our proposed method is based on raw data and does not rely on any hand-crafted features. To validate the efficacy of our approach, extensive experiments were conducted on the extended version of the DCASE2019 dataset. Our results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions, with significant improvements observed in localizing sound sources perpendicular to the microphone array axis.

Conventional wireless systems face limitations due to their susceptibility to interference when multiple signals are transmitted simultaneously, but the advent of concurrent transmission offers a breakthrough. By employing advanced techniques such as interference cancellation and suppression, simultaneous transmission can occur without traditional orthogonality requirements, leading to notable improvements in spectral efficiency and system flexibility. Despite the complexity and intricacy involved, concurrent transmission methods are gaining traction as the future of wireless systems, with the potential to surpass existing technologies like OFDMA. This review provides an in-depth examination of concurrent transmission-based systems, covering various modulation methods, cancellation and suppression techniques, and their applications in both single- and multi-user scenarios. Additionally, the review explores concurrent transmission's suitability for 6G and beyond systems and discusses the emerging areas of research within this domain.

Evaluating speech signal quality often involves examining spectrogram features, but current methods merely view them as a static snapshot, ignoring the inherent randomness of their construction. By capturing sonograms at evenly spaced time intervals, we demonstrate that their analysis collections follow a multivariate geometric distribution, enabling quality assessment through geometry-based techniques. The proposed method's accuracy matches state-of-the-art approaches, but with a significant computational advantage, making it feasible for real-time applications on resource-constrained devices.

Detecting the structure of a brain is crucial to understanding how it works. Researchers have been attempting to identify key patterns, such as stable wavefronts and neural clusters, within brain tissue using various techniques and algorithms. However, many existing approaches are impractical for real-world applications due to their high computational demands or low detection accuracy. Our team has developed a novel, universal method capable of identifying both stable and moving neural patterns through extensive simulations and thorough testing. Our results show that the Longitudinal Phase Gradient method performs better than alternative algorithms in most cases, revealing the stable frequencies of neural clusters with remarkable accuracy. Our findings also demonstrate that the LPG can effectively identify all components of complex brain patterns, such as the stable wavefronts and neural clusters within spiking ring networks, even when the network contains many neurons.

We present a novel execution for the N-body code REBOUND, utilizing a randomized forces approach to mitigate CPU cache misses, without modifying the underlying code. This revised execution yields a substantial improvement in CPU utilization, yielding up to a 40% performance gain, particularly for large simulations exceeding 1000 particles. By synchronizing REBOUND's time-step calculations with its data-driven COPERNICUS execution, we preserve the code's existing efficiency while enhancing it further.

Experimental scientists operating under stringent measurement constraints strive to maintain precise control over individual quantum systems to extract maximum information from them. This regulation is often achieved by adjusting system parameters in response to ongoing measurements, but current theoretical models fail to accurately describe this process, particularly in scenarios where the gain and loss rates are not negligible. By developing a quantum Fokker-Planck equation, we gain a deeper understanding of how feedback loops behave far from the standard approximation limits, and reveal surprising results, such as the dual-peak distribution of certain states and the non-monotonic nature of entanglement generation. These findings open the door to streamlined modeling techniques for operations involving feedback, and may guide the design of advanced quantum computing architectures, like error correction codes and externally controlled gates.

This study builds upon the findings of D\'uez and G\'eronimo's work on alternating sequences of blocked discs in one dimension with varying masses, examining the emergence of exponential small eigenvalues in the associated Jacobi operator. The current research extends this investigation to systems of alternating discs in two dimensions, where the distances between adjacent centers are significantly smaller than their radii, and where the residues (weights) of the associated Jacobi operator can differ. The examined configurations assume that all discs are separated from a specified half-plane by a plane, where the normals to this half-plane all point in the same hemispace. Given these settings, the research demonstrates that such configurations give rise to exponential small eigenvalues in the associated minimal Neumann Laplacian, with the eigenvalue magnitude dependent on the smallest disc's radius, its weight, and the impedances at the plane separation.

El Ni\~no events trigger significant alterations in global weather patterns, particularly affecting regions experiencing significant seasonal rainfall. Regions heavily dependent on seasonal rainfall are extremely vulnerable to El Ni\~no's impact, with some varieties of El Ni\~no events having the capacity to reverse the direction of wind systems, thereby producing either very low or elevated rainfall. This study delves into the distinct characteristics of these varied El Ni\~no types within the context of extremely low and elevated rainfall areas, uncovering evidence that their signatures are imprinted in the phases of sea level pressure anomalies over the tropics and subtropics, as well as in the circulation features of convective clouds resulting from cloud-related satellite data. Notably, the distinct signatures of these El Ni\~no types are particularly apparent in regions experiencing very low and elevated rainfall, where their identification and differentiation hold substantial importance.

Recent studies have revealed numerous massive black holes that appear to deviate significantly from the standard population, characterized by masses ranging from 10,000 to 100 million times that of the sun. These exceptional black holes could be the remnants of unique formation processes such as the collapse of ultramassive stars or primordial black holes created shortly after the Big Bang. Although their mass ranges overlap, current data is insufficient to definitively distinguish between these potential origins. By applying formation and evolution models to various populations of massive black holes, including those observed through gravitational wave detection and those residing in the centers of galaxies or globular clusters, researchers could identify distinct populations and identify the characteristics of those with lower masses. For instance, the population of unbound, field black holes identified by unassociated laser interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory events in the laser interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory Third data catalog suggests the existence of intermediate-mass black holes with masses around 1,000 to 10,000 times that of the sun. Similarly, a re-examination of the motion of a black hole candidate detected by laser interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory event GW190521 within the dwarf galaxy CW Leo A reveals that it is likely a stellar remnant rather than a black hole formed from the collapse of an ultramassive star, thanks to its low velocity and the high density of stars within the galaxy. In a three-dimensional material featuring Kagome crystallographic symmetry, the presence of flat bands near the Fermi level gives rise to unique magnetic field responses, such as a phenomenon where resistance increases with the magnetic field. Researchers examined the electronic properties of a multi-orbital model on a Kagome lattice, consisting of 3d transition metals and surrounding an f-electron impurity, and found that specific conditions within this model induce two distinct phenomena: (i) a flat band becoming unstable and causing the system to become metallic with frequent electron collisions, (ii) these collisions becoming increasingly less frequent as the material's carrier density decreases due to the impurity's strong magnetic fields, thus producing a phenomenon where resistance decreases with the magnetic field. Our results further reveal that among 35 binary alloys with Zn on the Kagome lattice and transition metal atoms at the crystal's tetrahedral sites, only materials containing certain 3d and 4d transition metals produce the phenomenon where resistance increases with the magnetic field, with these being V-Zn, V-Ru, Cr-Ru and Ni-Zn.

This study combines analysis of genome-wide association studies with functional genomics to identify key regulatory mechanisms influencing human traits and diseases. By integrating various chromatin states, transcription factor maps, and evidence from independent conformation analysis, we successfully pinpoint influential variants underlying associations in genome-wide association studies for 18 characteristics, integrating over 600,000 variants, and point to potential target genes and downstream influences on variant-associated characteristics.

A block design is characterized by a tuple $(v,b,r,k,\lambda)$ satisfying specific numerical conditions. We investigate flag-transitive designs that meet the condition of being coprime to $r$ and $\lambda$. Our investigation reveals that only designs meeting these criteria with efficient group actions are symmetric BIBDs or projective planes. Additionally, we explore potential exceptions to this characterization, requiring either prime parameters or $\lambda$ being the product of two primes in certain scenarios.

For confined helium-like atoms in one spatial dimension, entropies including von Neumann, Shanon, and Fisher information entropies are examined. Non-Coulombic confinements in addition to the Coulomb interaction are analyzed using the variational method to obtain accurate nonperturbative ground-state energies and wave functions for atoms of various confinement sizes. These entropies in the present model exhibit both correlation effects and the influence of the Coulomb interaction, often counteracting each other. As a result, multiple studies in this area are needed, with further investigations into entropies in different physical systems being among them.

The 20-year binary pulsar observation has been crucial in verifying the equivalence principle and general relativity with high precision. A previously widely-used approach for analyzing this data has been based on comparing the observed decay of the system with the predicted decay under general relativity. In this research, we reframe this extensive study to provide a more accurate representation of the data, addressing a previously unrecognized shortcoming. Furthermore, we address concerns regarding the potential systematic biases in the radio frequency timing data.

This paper offers revised interpretations of two pivotal transformations in multiplicative linear logic: the Removal and Cut-Removal rules. Initially developed by Glivenka in 1931, these transformations serve as essential tools for establishing correspondences between multiplicative linear logic and its classical counterpart. The revised evaluations not only confirm that both transformations preserve provability but also validate that they are definitive in nature.

Predicting the concurrent progression of time-based financial datasets is crucial for identifying synchronized turning points in their evolution. Traditional financial indicators often fail to capture nuanced relationships between concurrent datasets, which traditional methods may overlook. Our proposed method leverages Cross Recurrence Plots to capture complex dynamics and thus better predict synchronized behavior. The results of our computer simulations and real-world trials on financial markets and individual accounts demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

To analyze phonon impacts on open quantum systems, we incorporate the influence of momentum into the electron-phonon interaction model and utilize an exact method to derive a valid Hamiltonian in the high-momentum limit. This allows us to investigate the consequences of momentum on the phonon-induced decoherence process through a master equation in the high-momentum phonon perturbation framework. Our research focuses on the distinct effects of decoupled and coupled electron-vibrational interactions on the system's dynamics. Additionally, we explore how the electron-vibrational coupling alters the phonon-induced relaxation rates and demonstrate that in the weak decoupled scenario, phonon effects can induce vibrational excitation, thereby generating phonon phonons. Furthermore, in the presence of momentum, electron-vibrational coupling can amplify or diminish the relaxation rates, depending on the specific conditions. Finally, we examine the impact of spin-phonon coupling, finding that it induces spin dephasing and, in the presence of momentum, can induce spin relaxation. Moreover, in the presence of electron-vibrational coupling, the spin relaxation process exhibits more intricate patterns.

Predicting user interaction with search results is a critical aspect of enhancing the overall user experience, leading to increased engagement and revenue. The effectiveness of forecasting Click-Through-Rates (CTR) is largely dependent on understanding the relevance of the visual aspects presented in the results. In our approach, treating newly promoted results as black boxes limits our capacity to utilize visual elements to improve CTR predictions. Consequently, in scenarios involving visually rich promotions, our models tend to perform poorly. Addressing this limitation, we introduce a novel method for leveraging image content and create material embeddings that can be seamlessly integrated into existing models without compromising their performance on traditional queries. Our approach demonstrates a significant 2% enhancement in CTR prediction accuracy when applied to newly promoted searches, all the while maintaining the robustness of the existing models in other contexts.

This document introduces a set of technical constraints, known as cardinality restrictions, for IT cases in complex systems. The cardinality restrictions serve to limit the number of instances of Cases at a specific system complexity level, thereby defining the boundaries of decomposability among these cases. The cardinality restrictions can serve two main purposes: first, to enforce specific constraints on the granularity of the cases within a model, ensuring that the cases align with a predetermined level of detail; second, to identify the optimal level of detail for the cases within a model, thereby facilitating an efficient representation of the underlying system. The document provides formal definitions of cardinality restrictions and explores their implications for IT case management and system analysis.

Wildfires are a natural and widespread occurrence on Earth, producing significant amounts of man-made particulate matter through combustion processes that play a crucial role in the Earth's energy balance and atmospheric chemistry. Although satellite data can help wildfire experts predict and monitor fires, the use of this data for predictive and monitoring purposes is hindered by limited access and the lack of suitable data processing methods. To overcome these challenges, this research presents a novel physics-informed method that integrates statistical modeling, data-driven state estimation, and remote-sensing data feeds from multiple geostationary satellites to create a comprehensive understanding of wildfire and aerosate formation processes. By leveraging these multi-source data feeds, the proposed approach provides real-time and high-resolution observations of atmospheric conditions, including fire areas, particulate matter formation processes, air masses, and weather patterns, thereby providing valuable insights for wildfire and air quality forecasting.

This study investigates the tracking privacy of location data under the conditionally biased probability distribution, utilizing information theory.  We derive both quantitative and qualitative measures, including the conditional entropy and score functions, to evaluate tracking privacy.  Both metrics adhere to the principles of Le Cam's Scoring Function Theorem, demonstrating its broad applicability across diverse statistical models.  We examine specific scenarios, such as the location distribution of Geiger counter data, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed metrics.

The analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data is complicated by the complex, multi-component nature of brain signals. Current statistical methods, primarily based on linear correlations, are insufficient to manage the high dimensionality and sparse data inherent to rs-fMRI, which often leads to overestimated connection strengths and reduced temporal resolution compared to event-related designs. This research employs a novel Bayesian approach, incorporating multiple time-ordered site pairings, along with confidence intervals for each estimated relationship. Our method enables more accurate modeling of resting-state data, taking into consideration data sparsity and temporal dynamics. By comparing the strength of correlations in both frequentist and Bayesian frameworks, we found that the latter better captures the dynamic, lower-strength nature of resting-state data. Our results demonstrate that the novel Bayesian model significantly improves prediction precision and better aligns with the dynamic characteristics of rs-fMRI data.

Directed graphs of non-positive Ricci curvature were analyzed to demonstrate the existence and distinctiveness of a unique density function, referred to as a 'measure density', originating from a source point. Furthermore, it was proven that this density function satisfies an exponential limitation. Directed graphs with lower Ricci curvature underwent similar examination; nonetheless, under certain conditions regarding volume growth, it was shown that the density function would become infinitely large at certain points under certain probability measures. Nonetheless, it was also proven that under certain conditions regarding curvature and support radius, the density of measure would remain within a finite bound under all possible probability measures. Lastly, it was shown that certain properties in directed graphs with a specific curvature grew at least linearly, significantly in contrast to the $log$-growth observed in undirected graphs with positive curvature.

Recent advancements in handling code-mixing have been constrained by the limitations of language-agnostic embeddings, which obscure linguistic characteristics, and static positional encodings, unsuited to the variable nature of code-mixing. Research has indicated that relative positional encodings are more effective than their absolute counterparts. In response, we propose a novel positional encoding technique that utilizes relative distance between words, and recommend it for use in applications involving code-mixing. Additionally, we introduce a new deep learning model, PESTO, that leverages transformer architecture and relative positional encoding to improve the performance of NLP tasks in code-mixing languages. Dynamic positional encoding allows the model to adaptively learn the relative distance between words, and our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional absolute positional encoding by a significant margin, and can complement contextual embeddings in applications involving code-mixing.

The transition temperature of the H3S superconducting material exhibits significant variation with pressure, despite its structural stability across a wide pressure range, thereby necessitating the consideration of additional factors in the explanation of its mechanism. Utilizing the linear relationship between nitrogen in trisulfur and pressure, we investigated how varying pressure affects H3S's electronic structure and superconducting properties. Near the pressure point of 150 GPa, where a van Hove singularity occurs, our analysis shows substantial changes in the electronic structure, resulting in an unusually large pressure coefficient for the transition temperature. Furthermore, in this region, S isotopic substitution has an increasingly substantial impact on transition temperature, with the effect becoming substantial at 155 GPa. These dynamic changes in the pressure parameter cause the previously reported distinct behaviors of the pressure coefficient and isotopic substitution to merge into one continuous relationship, thus unifying these phenomena.

Fisher's concept of the mean impact (MI) of an attribute within sample data has long been used to identify discriminatory characteristics. Recent research MI is isometrically related to the total variation distance of predictive variables, leading to a comprehensive study of its properties across various probability distributions. This work shows that an MI-based approach can consistently estimate a population parameter under specific assumptions regarding model form and variable independence. Notably, this result holds without those assumptions being met. Furthermore, an MI-based method successfully tracks changes in population discrimination over time in a real-world data set from the US, effectively capturing the gradual improvement of black white wage equality during the 2000-2019 period. Due to its broad applicability and robustness, MI emerges as a significant metric for both descriptive and inferential purposes in the field of causal analysis.

Assisting human locomotion by providing external forces has the potential to reduce physical strain on individuals with mobility impairments as well as make it more attractive for healthy people to use external exoskeletons. By delivering propulsion-assisted forces in the forward direction, both early and late in the gait cycle, we've found that it facilitates smoother and more efficient movements through reduced joint power requirements and increased stability. Specifically, we observed that this assistance improves stability in both late stance and pre-swing by providing forward and medially-directed forces. To address limitations in existing approaches that provide propulsion-assisted forces in a fixed direction, we've developed an active compliance controller capable of dynamically adjusting the end-effector force field to deliver optimal assistance tailored to individual needs.

Re-establishing an object's original position and orientation in a three-dimensional space is a complex challenge due to the high rate of feature updates.  Traditional methods that utilize hand-crafted descriptors often struggle with their limited ability to adapt.  Recent advancements in deep learning have shown promise in improving dynamic feature extraction, yet they struggle with the scarcity of training data and the absence of a reliable reference framework.  To address these issues, our approach combines the benefits of hand-crafted features with a 3D surfel-based reference framework for dynamic re-localization.  Specifically, our method involves learning from extensive, generatively created scenes to construct a three-dimensional map, which is then utilized in the re-localization process.  The proposed system demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art techniques when evaluated on synthetic environments based on MonoMap and driving re-localization datasets.

Semi-supervised learning's primary goal is to effectively utilize both labeled and unlabeled data to achieve superior results with less reliance on extensive labeling efforts. To date, most semi-supsupervised learning methods have heavily depended on the inherent characteristics of individual data points, restricting their applicability to a broader range of tasks and models. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel federated semi-supervised learning framework incorporating unlabeled points as regularization terms. Through theoretical analysis, we examine the influence of unlabeled data points on model optimization and clarify the ambiguities present in semi-supervised learning optimization problems. We demonstrate through numerical experiments that our proposed method outperforms existing methods, especially in tasks involving more complex models and diverse data distributions. Additionally, the approach exhibits superior performance in addressing client data heterogeneity and model regularization during federated semi-supervised learning optimization.

This study investigates how the initial electromagnetic field affects second-long black hole-neutron star collisions. By using a simulation, researchers found that the initial electromagnetic field causes power emitted in gravitational waves to decrease, while increasing the power of the initial electromagnetic and magnetic energy. As a result, an electromagnetic outflow is created, which lasts about 100 milliseconds and has a power of 10 to the power of 51 ergs per second. This outflow contains a magnetic energy that could potentially trigger a short gamma-ray burst on its own. Moreover, the initial electromagnetic field arrangement affects neutron star deformation and the mass of the accretion disk that is created. Lastly, the study found that a stiffer equation of state in the neutron star results in increased gravitational wave power and accretion mass, as well as a higher energy release from the initial electromagnetic and magnetic components.

In 1990s, the second author introduced the concept of "curl" as a measure of the disorder of a vector field on a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary, which later became associated with the rotation speed of particles. This note aims to demonstrate that the curl function is indeed an invariant when considering orientation-preserving isometric transformations of the manifold. Furthermore, the frequency distribution of the curl function is proposed as a potential invariant for the manifold itself, potentially facilitating its classification. To achieve this, suitable mathematical tools and methods need to be developed and refined.

Building on Rall's work on Convergence of Numerical Methods for an Unbounded Interval of Arguments, this paper offers a broader framework that unifies various numerical approaches developed for approximating Dinchva and Batkhar's Q-procedure. Specifically, this framework guarantees that any numerical method producing a more accurate result than the Q-procedure itself will approach the Q-procedure's solution as the step size diminishes. This methodical approach has practical applications in the discrete approximation of Cauchy type and hyperbolic differential equations. As such, several specific methods are presented, including those devised by Dinchva and Batkhar, as well as methods developed by the authors in previous studies.

The recent interest in graphene optical plasmonics stems from its potential to manipulate electromagnetic fields at the nanoscale through resonant plasmons. Recent studies have shown that electromagnetic fields can be efficiently coupled with terahertz electromagnetic waves, notably by leveraging the plasmonic properties of graphene nanoparticles. This coupling enables enhanced interactions between light and matter, opening doors to various applications in the terahertz spectrum.

Data from over 70,000 European patients who experienced an acute myocardial infarction and received treatment through emergency departments between 2008 and 2018 were used to analyze typical recovery patterns. By taking into account variations based on age, sex, and pre-infarction treatment exposure, stepwise regression identified distinct milestones marking recovery progress and duration for each demographic group. The results revealed recovery durations ranging from 14 to 28 days, heavily influenced by treatment adherence and demographic factors. Notably, recovery periods did not exhibit symmetry and varied significantly across different groups, underscoring the presence of diverse subpopulations with unique recovery trajectories. These findings highlight the potential of considering typical recovery patterns in therapy duration decisions and recommend further research to explore treatment options aligned with recovery progress.

This research proposes and evaluates a strategic multi-agent cooperation framework for coordinatingConventional Network Agents (CNAs). Each CNA is a constrained computational unit capable of communicating over a communication network. Agents model various types of hardware restricted in their communication and computation resources. The framework employs a two-stage approach: local agents collaborate using their direct connections, forming a network subgraph, from where a centralized controller makes global decisions. We developed an algorithm to find the optimal network partitioning for the largest possible group of agents and verified its efficiency in finding near-optimal solutions. The framework was successfully applied to define and identify effective tactical strategies for a scenario involving TETURSO robots, demonstrating that it can support complex tactical planning even with limited computational and communicative capabilities.

Our investigation of how chiral magnetic effect influences charge-dependent azimuthal correlations in Pb-Pb collisions may help determine its presence. We examined all particles' momentum transverse and collision centrality, excluding the influence of the Chiral Magnetic Wave, by directly calculating and analyzing the system. The correlations were measured and analyzed in Pb-Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider during 2010 and 2011, at $\sqrt{\it{s}_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ of 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The results do not support the existence of an enhancement of three-particle correlations due to the Chiral Magnetic Wave and are consistent with the expectations based on jet quenching and balanced asymmetry modulation approaches.

Over 1.5 million crowd-based fundraising projects are created annually on major platforms like GoFundMe, allowing multiple indicators such as fundraising duration, created date, and project creation time to be analyzed. These projects are accompanied by a wealth of crowd activity data that can provide insights into the effectiveness of the projects. However, the impact of crowd flow and indicators on the success of these projects has been the subject of ongoing debate. Understanding these effects has significant implications, allowing researchers and practitioners to identify successful projects and learn from failures to improve future projects. Leveraging the vast data available on successful and failed projects, we analyze over 3.5 million projects across three distinct platforms, uncovering the hidden dynamics and correlations among crowd indicators and their impact on the success of the projects. Our findings provide valuable insights into the nature of crowd behavior and the factors that influence the effectiveness of the projects.

Traditional approaches of sharing threat intelligence are inefficient and costly, 
often requiring manual processes or centralized platforms. To address this, 
we've developed an intelligent system called CDIX, allowing organizations to share 
threat information and collaborate on network breach identification through deep learning.
However, using federated training for deep learning presents challenges due to the high computational resources and expertise required.
To overcome these difficulties, we've created a user-friendly platform that enables organizations to train complex models on their data without exposing sensitive information.
This innovative approach enables seamless collaboration and efficient use of computational resources, allowing for optimal model performance and data privacy.
We've evaluated our system's capabilities by conducting experiments on public and private datasets and found it outperforms existing solutions in breach detection accuracy.
To support users, we've provided extensive documentation and a web-based interface for managing cyber danger sharing and model collaboration.

Our research centers on the intricacies of multi-point robotic manipulation ordering, where robots' movement sequences can have far-reaching implications for efficiency and feasibility. Changing the manipulation order can substantially impact path length and robot collisions, ultimately making tasks impossible to complete. To tackle this complex problem, we've developed an approach that leverages a clustering-based method to evaluate potential manipulation order changes and quantify their influence through the Avaricious Value, which measures the relative impact of each manipulation on permutation variations. This has led to the creation of the Avaricious Clustering-Driven Manipulation Ordering (ACDMO) technique, which utilizes the Variational Influence Analysis (VIA) to identify crucial points that affect permutation variations and efficiently assess their impact, ultimately achieving a balance of optimality and computational speed.

This report details the initial results of CMOS SiMOSFETs known for their high si agility. A conventional 300mm CMOS process was used to manufacture these devices, which exhibited a unique ability to switch between conducting and blocking modes rapidly. Prior to the standard CMOS steps, the device structures were formed using specific diffusion and oxidation techniques, utilizing n-on-p and p-on-n configurations. The manufacturing process incorporated the standard CMOS complement of n-channel and p-channel transistors. Characterization of the SiMOSFETs involved both DC and RF measurements to assess their performance, yielding notable values for gate capacitance and resistance. For the n-channel SiMOSFET, the parameters were $5.6\times10^{-3}\Omega\cdot F$ and $0.05\Omega$, whereas for the p-channel SiMOSFET, they were $6.10\times10^{-3}\Omega\cdot F$ and $0.14\Omega$.

In cooperative settings, the ability of individuals to synchronize is a crucial factor in achieving high levels of mutual benefit. Our research explores how cooperative outcomes are influenced by variations in the cooperative parameters among team members and internal team connections. Using the Prisoner's Dilemma as a baseline, we analyzed two-dimensional teams and found that differences in the temptation parameter lead to reduced team cohesion and lower payoffs. The impact is more pronounced in teams with diverse parameter sets and team members not connected within the network. Our study reveals that free riders can arise even in situations where the majority of team members are inclined towards cooperation. When considering teams consisting of interconnected individuals, our research indicates that mutualistic outcomes are more likely if both team members have similar inclinations towards cooperation. The impact of parameter diversity on these outcomes varies depending on whether the team is comprised of interconnected individuals or not. The findings are also applicable in the context of three-player games, such as when studying duos versus trio groups.

Upcoming virtual agents will be able to respond to text-based queries by streaming pre-recorded video from a diverse range of sources, like news broadcasts, sports events, and educational content. Although these agents could be beneficial, relying on a single source for all responses might introduce significant bias. To address this issue, we have developed a method to measure source variability bias in video-based reasoning, using a dataset of 321 pre-recorded responses from four distinct pre-specified sources. The results show that current video reasoning models are highly susceptible to source bias, with some sources producing significantly better performance than others. Notably, the effect size of this source variability for both zero-shot and fine-tuned models was measured and found to be substantial. The bias is largely attributed to training data bias, which we suggest could be mitigated by utilizing datasets with more balanced representation of the different pre-recording sources. The framework we have established for assessing source variability bias in video-based reasoning can be applied to evaluate bias in other multi-source datasets.

A Monodromy Anomaly in n=1 superspace was pinpointed as the source of a disparity between compactly compactified Wess-Zumino models in four dimensions and their four-dimensional hypermultiplet equivalents. Through re-supersymmetrization into Wess-Zumino models with non-trivial topology, we reconciled the anomalies, eliminating the obstruction and compacting the difference into a supersymmetric counterterm tied to the topology's monodromy. Employing the bootstrap method on the monodromy amplitude, we derived its explicit form and confirmed its relationship to the superconformal R-current's anomaly. Furthermore, we resolved the massless compactification obstructions in the vector multiplet and explored the bootstrap's application to further understanding the compactified theories' S-matrix properties.

We define and analyze an elliptic surface $E/\mathcal{K}$ over a Galois field $q$ (where $q$ is 2, 3, 5, 7, or 11) with exceptional fibers, exhibiting points on the elliptic curve $E(\mathbb{F})$ of orders 24, 48, 60, 84, and 120 respectively. We leverage this information to determine generators for $E(\mathbb{F})$. Furthermore, we consider three cyclic cubic fields $\mathbb{K}_i$ over $\mathbb{F}$, extending $E$ to $E_i$ defined over each $\mathbb{K}_i$. For these extensions, $E_i$ possesses points of orders 48, 84, and 120 respectively. Finally, we discovered that $E_3$ has points defined over $\mathbb{K}_3$ with orders 12 and 20, and we established that $E_3$ has a Mordell-Weil rank of 13 over $\mathbb{K}_3$.

Current stochastic medium access methods like CSMA/MA have inherent limitations
in managing interference within wireless networks, often resulting in low average
throughput and heightened variance. To address these issues, we propose a novel
interference-aware channel access method rooted in the Bernoulli schedule
framework. Leveraging medium access probability adjustments, this approach grants
different stations varying access probabilities on any given time slot, allowing
stations with less interference relationships a higher access probability. Thus,
this technique effectively manages interference relationships and enhances overall
network performance. Utilizing an interference matrix, we derive closed-form equations
for key performance metrics, including average throughput, throughput variance, and
delay, enabling precise evaluation without simulations. Subsequently, we develop a
flow control algorithm leveraging these analytical results to optimize flow scheduling
and medium access probability adjustment, ultimately maximizing network utility.

For node classification in large graphs, it's often impractical to gather sufficient labels. Recent approaches employ pseudo-tagging to address this issue, using semi-supervised learning to expand the label set with unsupervised nodes. However, pseudo-tags can introduce errors from unsupervised nodes, hindering performance when using these labels for training graph neural networks. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel approach that utilizes pseudo-tags as data annotations for node representation learning and conditional distribution estimation rather than accurate tags. By doing so, we can mitigate the impact of inaccurate pseudo-tags and achieve better performance with few real labels.

Video template matching has been the backbone of long-time video surveillance systems, 
enabling the detection and tracking of objects of interest, or templates. However, 
video matching has been a challenging problem, often resulting in low frame-per-second 
rates due to its computationally intensive nature. We present a new approach, 
short-distance template corresponding or PatchNet, which focuses on efficient 
template matching over short time intervals within a pyramidal approach. Our method 
involves dividing videos into short segments and applying a flow-field-guided approach 
to facilitate efficient template matching. Our research demonstrates that PatchNet 
outperforms existing methods, offering better outcomes, and better computational and 
storage efficiency, while only targeting short-distance template matching.

We modify the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process by introducing periodic boundaries at multiple points. The system's evolution is analyzed in the large system limit using the method of generalized hydrodynamics. The model features several types of exclusion processes and an additional contribution arising from the boundaries, which can be treated as a special case of the exclusion process with moving boundaries. The resulting interface describing the moving boundaries is analyzed for various multi-point configurations, particularly those involving the interplay of different phases within the exclusion process and the notable phenomenon where the interface moves away from the boundaries in the short term and then converges in the long term.

A novel wireless communication method called SWIPT enables a single radio signal to be used for both transmitting and harvesting energy. In an uplink multi-service system that leverages SWIPT, this work investigates how to optimally allocate the downlink energy transfer protocol parameters and the uplink total power among various users to maximize overall system throughput while ensuring minimum energy harvesting per user through both routes. To achieve this optimal resource allocation, two iterative algorithms based on iterative convex approximation are developed to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem by breaking it into manageable sub-problems. Furthermore, by applying Dinkelbach's algorithm, the non-convex fractional programming problem can be solved efficiently using the proposed Dinkelbach's algorithm along with the corresponding solution methods for its sub-problems as well as an alternative method utilizing semidefinite relaxation. The effectiveness and superiority of the proposed solutions over a method that disregards the coupling effect are confirmed through numerical simulations as well as theoretical analysis via Lagrange multipliers.

This study delves into the implications of non-standard SU(N) Fermi mixtures that exhibit a specific quark content $[(u_1\bar d)^N+(u_2\bar d)^N+\ldots+(u_N\bar d)^N]$. Although theoretically constrained to even N values, we explore the concept of $N$-way quantum interference in electron systems. Our analysis examines how these finite-N configurations are influenced by the interactions between the two types of Fermi particles involved ($u_1\bar d$ and $u_2\bar d$), with a focus on the effects of repulsive interactions. To this end, we investigate how the system's wave function is impacted by both weak and strong repulsive interactions, particularly in the presence of strong interactions where the wave function is limited to zero overlap. To overcome the limitations imposed by Pauli's exclusion principle, we investigate the influence of a tunable width parameter. Our research reveals that both scenarios, with weak and strong repulsive interactions, exhibit varying responses depending on the SU(N) Fermi mixture configuration and the exclusion width, with overlap being particularly minimal in strong repulsive interactions and specific N-content configurations. In contrast, weak repulsive interactions exhibit varying overlap depending on the Fermi momentum and specific N-content configurations, exhibiting overlap only when an odd number of Fermi momenta match one another. Ultimately, our research highlights unique physical properties arising from non-standard SU(N) Fermi mixtures

We've developed a novel electrical circuit representation of optomechanical systems that rely on materials with a meta-atomic structure. The model incorporates classical oscillators representing light and mechanical movements, coupled through capacitors that emulate the mediating role of photons in the interaction. Unlike quantum-circuit approaches that use entangled qubits, our analysis stands on solid empirical ground with clear analogies between electrical and photonic concepts. We demonstrate how this electrical analogy can be applied to understand the behavior of coherent coupling and explore its impact on mechanical stability and system dynamics.

Starting from the definition of universal semi-circle polynomials, a set of universal Airy polynomials is developed using the same recursive structure. The leading coefficients of these universal polynomials correspond to the leading coefficients of the classical Poincaré polynomials for unitary group and unitary Grassmannian, as well as those of the classical Airy polynomials for symmetric matrix ranges, which in turn correspond to unitary group, symmetric matrices and orthogonal Grassmannian classes. The results show that these leading coefficient polynomials possess exceptional orthogonality properties with respect to four different weight functions, and similar properties apply to the full polynomials under specific conditions.

Mobile robots that climb vertical surfaces rely on predictable environments.
However, in heterogeneous settings, the environments the robots navigate in can
drastically change due to differing surface properties, which makes it hard for
the robots to maintain equilibrium on their own. This paper presents a planar
glass barrier that introduces unpredictable changes in adhesion, varying by both
position and orientation. Robots navigating along this barrier will experience
shifts in equilibrium positions when the adhesion changes, even when there are
no external disturbances present. An inverted pendulum with variable mass is
used to model the behavior of a clip-on-style robot, allowing us to analyze the
stable regions the robot can operate in under differing adhesion conditions.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects within 2dcftQFT by extending it to globally hyperbolic spacetimes and integrating it with causal structures. The study achieves this by constructing caustically restricted causal functions on a given manifold M, with these functions forming a subalgebra of the QFT's algebra of functionals. The algebra of caustically restricted functions is then shown to satisfy homotopy-isomorphism with the full algebra, indicating structural equivalence. The study then focuses on massless scalar field QFT and its functional algebra, with the study of caustically restricted functional appearing as a theory of "chiral QFTs." The article then generalizes these findings to QFTs defined on arbitrary globally hyperbolic spacetimes M, showing that caustically restricted functional algebras in these spacetimes are homotopy-isomorphic to the full algebra of the respective QFT.

Recent research highlights the significance of computer vision techniques in endoscopic surgery to facilitate surgical procedures and improve patient outcomes. However, the complexity and costliness of deep learning models pose challenges for their implementation. Most recent deep learning smoke detection models rely on extensive training datasets, which are costly to create and time-consuming to annotate. Furthermore, the poor visual quality in laparoscopic surgery hampers their performance. To address these issues, a novel two-stage model combining image enhancement and smoke detection has been proposed. The first stage involves the application of an image improvement method to optimize visual clarity, and the second stage entails using this enhanced model to create smoke detection templates. By leveraging these templates, real-time inference can be achieved without the need for retraining. Additionally, a novel method for fine-tuning these models is introduced to minimize the need for annotation. The proposed model demonstrates improved performance over current state-of-the-art models and exhibits strong scalability properties.

To minimize errors in multi-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions, we need to achieve noise-free motion. We present a technique that allows the MS gate to function effectively across a wide range of motional frequencies by having the driving lasers excite the ion's movements independently in phase and amplitude. By doing this, we eliminate the need for motion cooling and frequency sensing, allowing the gate to be executed swiftly even in noisy conditions. Our results show the gate can function reliably up to 100 dB of motion noise.

The mechanism behind the paraelectric phase in titanium dioxide and similar materials has been debated for a long time due to experimental limitations in verifying structural models, which in turn affects the understanding of the phase transition into the ferroelectric phase. Employing advanced technology that enables the visualization of atomic arrangements in microscopic images, this research demonstrates that a previously proposed model of the structure of titanium dioxide and similar materials does not align with the experiment results. Conversely, the experiment supports the characteristics of the proposed ferroelectric phase model, which suggests that a specific type of ion displacement is necessary for the phase transition to occur.

Two distinct methods for analyzing multivariate functional data were previously developed under the names Functional Gaussian Graphical Models and Graphical Gaussian Processes. Although they were based on the same underlying statistical model, their relationships were previously unclear. In our research, we demonstrate that these two approaches are, in fact, equivalent, but manifest differently based on the nature of the domain being discrete or continuous. Furthermore, we developed a new functional multivariate regression model, known as Graphical Gaussian Process Regression, and showed that it has a direct counterpart, Graphical Functional Linear Models, through its expansion on a multivariate conditional kernel.

As quantum computing advances, accurately tracing and debugging quantum programs becomes increasingly challenging due to the rapid growth of their corresponding quantum circuit diagrams. Currently, quantum editing tools fall short in addressing this issue. Despite their importance, common belief holds that addressing this problem requires significant advancements in graph theory. We tackle this challenge by developing innovative and efficient methods for assembling quantum circuits featuring recurring patterns, thereby facilitating the simplification of complex quantum programs through novel structural insights and recurring sub-patterns. Our approach, rooted in fundamental graph theory principles and standard programming strategies, opens up the realm of meaningful structural analysis and editing for quantum circuits. Through numerical evaluations on real quantum computing platforms, our solutions exhibit notable performance improvements, offering up to an 8-fold enhancement in efficiency. Our findings empower practitioners with reliable techniques for managing large-scale quantum circuits and paving the way for further exploration of graph-based analysis and editing in this domain.

The primary objective of this research is to establish average-case tail dominance phenomena in various convex models of statistical learning. Our findings reveal that certain average-case scenarios exhibit tail dominance, even within the most basic frameworks of convex analysis, surpassing even the most robust multicorrelated regimes. The proof methodology employed relies on innovative techniques of analytic convex geometry and includes novel insights into typical behavior within hyperplane arrangements. The underlying probability distributions in these models display exceptional strong concentration, characterized by distinct "poorpoorpoor" tails, which are indicative of robust convexity. The results of this study have implications for understanding both theoretical and practical instances of statistical learning tasks.

Our study delves into the energy aspects of polaron formation in unconstrained bilayer systems, where the electron and hole don't necessarily reside within distinct layers. By examining bilayer systems with varying dielectric screening and electrostatic layer spacing, we investigate their impact on binding energy. Furthermore, our research also analyzes the consequences of polaron formation on ionization energy and energy gaps. Notably, polaron formation has a substantial influence on the latter aspect, and in certain cases, can even induce excitons to become superconducting. This phenomenon marks the first instance of excitonic polaron analysis in bilayer systems and opens up new possibilities for excitonic superconductivity in bilayer systems.

In recent years, Locating and Tracking Entities (LTE) has become increasingly significant due to the growing reliance on real-time localization and tracking in various fields, including autonomous driving and robotics. PDA techniques utilizing radio signals are well-established in 4G/5G networks for accurate localization, but they are highly susceptible to interference from in-band signals. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages communication transfer to facilitate real-time localization and tracking even in the presence of interference signals. The proposed technique uses a simplified radio map to identify and filter out interference signals, while accurately extracting channel features for position estimation. Our results demonstrate its effectiveness with an average error reduction of 0.33 meters compared to existing methods.

The complex polarisation states of particle pairs, $W^{\pm}Z$, produced through proton-proton interactions, are examined at a high-energy collision of 13 TeV. This research is grounded in a substantial dataset with a collision accumulation of 137 fb$^{-1}$, captured by the ATLAS detector. This analysis marks the first time all-polarisation states of these particle combinations have been observed, and their real-world occurrences are compared with predictive Standard Model simulations. This comprehensive study enables an in-depth exploration of the fundamental weak forces at play.

The Cotton tensor emerges naturally from a symmetric, rank-3 gravitational tensor derived independently of the Einstein tensor. Although it vanishes upon contraction, its fully covariant form contains information essential to a consistent gravitational theory. When analyzed in an inertial frame, this form reveals a gravitational potential energy with a force that attracts masses at rates inversely proportional to the square of their separation distance, offering a new perspective on the gravitational field's physical properties.

Building upon the foundational concept by Borcegno and Casati, we broadened the definition of a spectral lattice to apply to orthocomplemented lattices with a substantial application in quantum logic. Our work extends spectral orthomodular lattices to include orthospectral lattices, and similarly, orthospectral ortholattices. The implications of these concepts are explored through the establishment of categorical equivalences. Specifically, we demonstrate the equivalence between the category of spectral ortholattice frames and the category of spectral ortholattice spaces, and the equivalence between the category of orthospectral ortholattice frames and the category of orthospectral ortholattice spaces.

We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into an image format, facilitating easy comprehension and verification of complex mathematical arguments. By representing each step in a proof as a node in a directed graph, with corresponding Coq command labels, our system enables the reconstruction of the original proof approach. This graph can then be rendered as an image, revealing the underlying logical flow and structural relationships within the proof. Building on previous work [Kouwenberg, Ouwehand, Bruijn, Tijms, '20], our updated system supports a broader range of data types and data structure operations originally introduced in [Kouwenberg, Ouwehand, Bruijn, Tijms, '18].

We demonstrate that the maximum fourth moment of normalized analytic Hecke cusp forms over any fixed range of conductor is precisely bounded above by $N^{1/2+\epsilon}$ for all values of $N$. This result nearly resolves a conjecture proposed by Soundararajan in 2011, with the exception of the exponent being off by $0.026$. This finding also exactly settles a related hypothesis initially proposed by Iwaniec and Kowalski in their 2006 text.

Interior Point Methods (IPMs), particularly those based on Newton's method, continue methodically until two specific conditions are met: the optimality and feasibility of the solution are fully achieved. A significant limitation of these methods is that determining when to terminate under the feasibility condition is complicated due to issues such as infinite values or complex data structures like sparse matrices. Research indicates that employing a relative error framework can mitigate this problem, yet most solutions involve resolving intricate nonlinear equations, which is costly. The proposed solution involves utilizing an absolute error framework, paired with an overestimation approach that simplifies the feasibility residual without overemphasizing infinite values. This innovative approach allows for straightforward evaluation of the residual, eliminating the need to resolve complex equations, and consequently enhances the IPM solver's performance by streamlining its overall computational efficiency.

We have computed the first moment of the longitudinal splitting function $g_{L,\Omega=1}(x,\alpha_s)$ to $O(\alpha_s^4)$ in variable flavor number scheme, and the first moment of the transversality splitting function $g_{T,\Omega=1}(x,\alpha_s)$ to $O(\alpha_s^3)$ in the same scheme, and found that they vanish respectively.

Understanding limitations posed by real-world complexities requires comprehensive insights into various environmental factors. Presently, most AI incident repositories are absent, while unsuitable ones exist, hindering effective learning from mistakes made by AI systems in practical settings. To bridge this comprehension gap, we propose the AI Incident Repository (AIIR), a comprehensive database documenting limitations encountered by AI systems in real-world applications. AIIR encompasses $516$ incidents from six diverse real-world domains, in which AI systems experienced failures or setbacks. Each entry in the repository is annotated with explanatory details, facilitating researchers to analyze patterns and understand contextual nuances. Furthermore, utilizing AIIR, AI systems' performance is evaluated on providing city-level weather forecasts, highlighting instances where they struggle to accurately predict extreme events like heavy snowfall. The inclusion of AIIR can augment current training datasets, enhancing AI systems' functionality in practice. The repository is accessible at https://incident-ai.net/

We've developed an accurate method to numerically solve the renormalization group differential equation in real-space, overcoming many limitations of earlier approaches that relied on approximations or complex transformations. Our approach enables researchers to bypass these hurdles and apply the renormalization group directly to complex, high-dimensional systems with complex interaction structures. We've successfully applied this method to model diffusion and dynamics in disordered systems and also exact solvers like the Harris-Chayes RNG, demonstrating an alternative way to obtain precise solutions and offering potential new insights into system behavior.

Human interaction design often relies on dual-process specifications which posit that users adhere to intuitive behaviors as specified in requirements, assuming these behaviors are natural and self-evident. Building upon this concept, recent advancements within automated dispute resolution have enabled the automatic detection of specifications that do not align with observed interactions. Despite these developments, several important research questions remain unresolved. Our study tackles these unanswered inquiries by utilizing automata theory to formulate dispute management techniques that not only identify but also rank the most frequently disputed specifications according to their frequency of violations. Furthermore, we provide practical examples that illustrate the application of these techniques in real-world scenarios.

We define the computational model for the theoretical machine language of a weak Qubit model called Proto-Machine. This theoretical machine is then used to justify a weak correspondence theorem, which in turn supports the main correspondence theorem of Quipper. By analyzing Proto-Machine, we develop a practical compiler that compiles Proto-Quipper-M programs into the theoretical machine language. The analysis of the compiler's correctness leads to the demonstration of its correctness.

Utilizing an unconstrained ensemble of random matrices with entries defined by a fully independent and identically distributed distribution, we derive an approximate description of the largest eigenvalues beyond the main spectral limit. For distributions symmetric around zero, it is demonstrated that the extreme eigenvalues independently follow identical distributions. Similarly, for asymmetric distributions with a finite mean, the extreme eigenvalues also independently follow identical distributions. Furthermore, by examining the behavior of these distributions near critical points - which occur when the symmetry or the third moment conditions are breached - critical phenomena arise. Specifically, both the distribution parameters and the density of states exhibit power-law behavior at these critical points. Furthermore, it is shown that in certain critical cases, the joint distribution of the largest eigenvalues can be exactly described.

A proposed optical phase assessment technique exploits the correlation between long-lived atomic dipoles and the photons they emit from an enclosed cavity. The phase is estimated by analyzing the dipole's output light, facilitated by a sophisticated preparation process that creates pairs of bosonic excitations within the dipole system through rapid pulse stimulation. The phase is then inferred from the modified dipole dip correlations, obtained at varying delay times, following a modulated and interrupted stellar stimulus. The phase is ultimately estimated by comparing the dipole dip correlation peaks against corresponding simulated data. The proposed technique's feasibility and precision boundaries are evaluated based on the characteristics of the cavity-dipole system under consideration.

As a crucial step in genome assembly processes, creating a distributed memory parallel counter has proven to be an intricate task due to the challenge of avoiding data duplication and maintaining cache efficiency. Previous strategies for addressing this issue either led to suboptimal cache utilization or involved complex programming. In this study, we introduce a novel solution to this problem that utilizes the inherent features of the CPU cache and involves no redundant memory access. This innovative approach has been integrated into the wtdbg2 assembler for constructing de novo assemblies of whole genomes and has been successfully applied to multiple genome genomes, including human, and other diverse genomes, to demonstrate its efficiency. Furthermore, the approach has been compatible with various Creations.

A modified logistic equation incorporating a time delay represents the fundamental model of population dynamics in biology. This paper explores a new equation with a population dynamics delay logistic term and derives conditions under which solutions remain bounded, positive, and globally attractive. These conditions are then applied to understand the global behavior of the equation in light of recent delays in biology.

The traditional Depth framework deals with data depth measurement for data matrices.
The conventional approach relies on the data matrix's assumption, but real-world data
often deviates from this norm. To address this issue, this paper generalizes the Depth
paradigm for point procedures using the Isometric Log-Change transformation and
demonstrates the efficacy of the resulting depth measurements with spherical and elliptical
distributions.

Achieving optimal performance in hybrid superconducting quantum devices hinges on managing interfaces between diverse components. By applying rigorous principles to model each layer and interface and utilizing well-proven fabrication techniques, nearly perfect device behavior can be attained. Building on this idealized framework, we can isolate the intrinsic limitations of various architectural designs and even achieve near-perfect qubit purity. Although such perfect devices may not be fully realizable, they serve as valuable benchmarks for evaluating and refining practical devices. As noted by David Pashke for the aphorism, 80% of the ideal represents 100% of the practical.

Researchers employed a high-resolution magnetic spectrometer to analyze the atomic masses of various Germanium isotopes - specifically, $^{56,57,58,59,60}$Ge - near the $N$ = 40 neutron shell closure. The study utilized a precise method involving a 48Ca beam and multiple targets at the CSNSRIM research facility in Japan.
