and time-consuming for local authorities. This research presents a transfer
learning framework to overcome these limitations by leveraging data from multiple
countries.A framework is proposed to efficiently identify road damages using a
transfer learning approach, leveraging data from multiple countries. This approach
involves two types of transfer learning - feature transfer - and model transfer - to overcome differences
between datasets, followed by fine-tuning to enhance model performance on local data.
A proposed framework also incorporates transfer learning - transfer in distribution - to harmonize data,
ensuring that variations among datasets do not hinder the effective use of machine learning models.
After applying this approach, road damage classification models are developed and compared against
existing models, demonstrating that transfer learning can improve overall performance and mitigate
discrepancies caused by variations among data sources.

I demonstrate that a generative model can be developed using data from a different domain and serve as a bridge to produce policies that replicate the dynamics of an target domain.  This approach proves particularly beneficial in adapting to new environments with distinct physics, differing from the ones in which most deep RL algorithms are trained.  The proposed method mimics the dynamics of a new domain by observing solely without requiring labeled data.  The policy's success does not rely on the similarity between the target and training domains.  The method's effectiveness is validated through training on pixels for locomotion in MuJoCo and further cross-domain tests in Habitat.  The policy's success does not rely on labeled data.

To investigate the impact of magnetic fields on disk formation around Population III protostars, we conducted a series of simulations, incorporating population III protostar gravity into an existing magnetohydrodynamics code. A series of simulations, labeled P3D1 through P3D5, explored various initial entropy conditions and magnetic field strengths in spherical symmetry, using a resolution up to 200 times the gravitational radius and a magnetic field up to the equipartition level. Our results indicate that weak magnetic fields, comparable to the Alfv\'en number in the first stars, promote collapse and cooling without the formation of a disk. Conversely, strongly ordered, intense magnetic fields, comparable to the equipartition level, can suppress cooling, promote shock-driven hydrogen line emission, and lead to fragment formation at radii 10 to 100 times the gravitational radius. These fragments may be mitigated over time as angular momentum is transferred outward through magnetic tension, ultimately resulting in the fragmentation of the protostellar disk.

This study focuses on the association rule analysis, a pivotal component of data mining, which enables the detection and characterization of dependencies within datasets. It's crucial to note that association rules derived from the same dataset exhibit varying degrees of redundancy, influencing their computational efficiency and interpretability. Consequently, this paper delves into the concept of redundancy among association rules, introducing a novel framework for categorizing and inducing sets of nonredundant rules. Building upon this framework, we introduce a structured approach to generating minimal bases, a long-standing goal in association rule mining. This framework enables the determination of minimal bases with controlled size and number elements, and we illustrate its practical application with an algorithm. Furthermore, we provide guarantees on the maximum length of rules in this structured approach and assess its computational complexity.

A mandatory therapy system within prisons aims to address the mental health needs of inmates and reduce disciplinary issues through voluntary sessions with mental health professionals. We investigate its effects on inmates' mental health and behavior, using psychological tests and prison division statistics. Our analysis utilizes a difference-in-differences approach with microdata from a well-structured prison. In addition, we examine the therapy system using macrodata to study possible selection biases and exploit variations among prisons. Our findings show that participating in compulsory therapy leads to improved psychological well-being, measured by standardized tests, specifically benefiting those with initial mental health issues. Despite this improvement, inmates' behavior within the prison does not show a corresponding decline. There is also no evidence of staff or inmates manipulating therapy enrollment for personal gain.

This study derives distinct types of parametric Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials from the corresponding parametric generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials and establishes their defining properties and recurrence relations. Additionally, corresponding generating functions are identified. We also examine specific parametric types of generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials and their associated real-valued types. This work extends the results of [S. Akkurt, S. Ozden, S. Yildirim, Type-apostol-Bernoulli parameters and their properties. Adv. Stud. Theor. Phys. 11 (2017) 155-164.](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-58188-1_12) and references therein.

This study introduces the concept of radio chart estimation by independent unmanned aerial vehicles and proposes corresponding estimation algorithms. The mathematical framework for radio signal measurement is developed, taking into account the differences between UAV positions, building environments, and frequency variations. Three practical assumptions are conceived to enhance the understanding of radio signal estimation, encompassing signal stability, line-of-sight behavior, and uncertainty in sensing. The non-linear nature of the estimation problem leads to an unsolvable equation system. The problem is demonstrated to be NP-hard through reduction. The paper presents two algorithms for radio chart estimation and evaluates their effectiveness in ensuring accurate UAV operations and situational awareness in complex environments.

This research introduces a novel HMM-based approach to anomaly detection that utilizes examination of transition and emission probabilities. We argue that traditional anomaly detection methods focused on sequence probability, such as those used in the HMM, VQ, and DCT approaches, often suffer from high false positive rates and ANORB is one of them. In contrast, our proposed approach allows for the identification of anomalies that deviate significantly in behavior, not just in sequence. By looking for sequences that significantly differ from the normal in terms of probability, we can effectively detect anomalies. We enhance the HMM method by introducing a new performance metric to evaluate gauge probability and identify the most suitable model parameters. Furthermore, our results show that using four to five states in the HMM yields optimal outcomes, and reducing model complexity through a simplified HMM with uniform emissions and a single Fuzzy Clustering step improves computational efficiency without compromising accuracy.

This research introduces a novel individual authentication system that utilizes audio-visual-thermal sensors. Unlike conventional methods, this approach combines these distinct modalities to enhance accuracy and robustness. Specifically, the system uses visual and thermal cameras to collect data on individuals' facial attributes, audio sensors to capture voiceprints during speaking and facial movements during vocalization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system using a publicly available dataset and propose new features using cross-modal similarity metrics that outperform existing visual, thermal, and audio features. Furthermore, our study offers new insights into leveraging audio-visual-thermal sensing technology for enhanced and more secure individual identification.

Real-world data is frequently marred by distortions such as noise, altering its informational value. While speech signals can be enhanced, translating this improvement to text loses the connection between the two, rendering conventional methods ineffective. To address the issue of low-quality data, we introduce a text-to-text approach called data augmentation that minimizes effort and optimizes the value of the enhanced text. Our approach generates the most coherent and informative text possible given the original text and a chosen subset to be enhanced. To this end, we employ a dual-framework combining a data augmentation model and a language model. The speech-to-text model is updated to integrate the insights from both the original and augmented training data. Our approach yields significant improvement in the automatic speech recognition system's performance when applied to speech-recognition pre-trained models.

Evaluating the average value of parameters from different populations is crucial in generalized linear models where parameters are estimated using methods such as Bayesian estimation, maximum likelihood or moment estimation.  Several approaches have been proposed in the literature but often rely on the assumption of equal population sizes, which is not always the case in practical applications.  Assumptions about population sizes can be subjective and unreliable.  In contrast, our method does not rely on such assumptions and provides a way to estimate population averages without them.  The benefits of our approach are demonstrated through simulations and a real-world data set involving sample selection.

One-sided differential privacy models the scenario where a central authority shares data with users. It has its roots in data release situations like rating systems and credit scoring, where characteristics of individuals depend on each other. In order to protect information related to these interactions, we suggest a new framework for one-sided differential privacy that ensures the privacy of relationships between users and their data. We define novel definitions for multi-characteristic one-sided differential privacy that protect sensitive information about how users' characteristics interact. We then investigate theoretical limitations imposed by these definitions, proving that maintaining the privacy of multiple characteristics simultaneously results in multiplicative utility loss. We apply our framework to common statistical methods such as mean estimation and maximum likelihood analysis and provide precise estimates of utility loss resulting from特征 simultaneously.

We conducted an analysis of gas and dust distribution in the developing system AS 209, taking place at various spatial scales, particularly focusing on the boundary between its disk and wind. A distinct area of approximately 150 astronomical units features reduced gas emission and a significant amount of dust, indicating substantial mass loss from the disk. This unique feature is thought to be the site of gas and angular momentum loss, crucial to disk evolution. Despite detailed observations and data collection, the cause of reduced CO emission within this area remains uncertain. We examined two plausible explanations: angular momentum removal through physical processes or chemical transformations of molecules. Our study found that angular momentum loss through gas dynamics is insufficient to account for the observed data. Conversely, we found that the amount of lost CO to be consistent with observations if we consider the transformation of CO into CO2 through oxidation by atomic oxygen available in the system's wind.

We developed an evaluation framework for time-stamped availability data, which is crucial for understanding service reliability and evaluating customer support under varying time constraints. Our system comprises three integrated components: (a) an effective analytical framework, utilizing time-window-based evaluation, that incorporates time and effort as interconnected dimensions; and (b) an effective digital toolkit, consisting of a custom application and software functions, that streamlines analytical process through time and effort trade-offs; and (c) a standard reporting feature, enabling clear communication of findings through customized and multi-dimensional reports highlighting key indicators such as availability, conditional availability, and average support response time. By addressing methodological and practical challenges in timeStamped data analysis, our approach aids stakeholders in making informed decisions when balancing support efforts and user needs within specific time frames. The proposed digital tool facilitates flexible analysis options to better serve different stakeholder requirements.

By demonstrating that average field games involving controls constrained by state limitations can be resolved with gentle solutions, we establish a useful framework for analyzing games of controls with jumps resulting from limited dynamics.

High-density stellar clusters serve as crucial environments for observing the early stages of stellar formation and evolution in the galaxy disc. Recent advancements have enabled more efficient use of data from existing archives, leading to more reliable cluster member selection. This study further refines these methods by incorporating newly obtained Gaia EDR3 data, resulting in a more accurate dissolving time measurement for young clusters. A thread-like pattern emerges when plotting the dissolving times of all selected clusters against their age, revealing clusters that have not yet begun to dissolve. These clusters are heavily concentrated at the newly established threshold of 30 million years old, a key finding that challenges the long-held belief that clusters start forming at 10 million years old. Instead, clusters tend to survive for an average of 30 million years, a number more closely aligned with the mass of individual stars rather than initially forming in dense cluster environments. This discovery suggests that the majority of stars in the galaxy formed not within these dense environments, but rather as solitary stars or members of loose stellar groups. Ultimately, this implies that the vast majority of stars in the galaxy formed as they do today: scattered across the disc, primarily as individual stars rather than dense clusters.

Producing fashionable clothing items requires not only adhering to current trends but also ensuring consistency across all pieces in a batch. Defining inconsistency in fashion, however, remains a complex task due to its subjective nature. We introduce Visual inconsistency detection for Clothing retailers with Transformer and Fashion-oriented contrastive pre-training, a novel framework for automatically identifying fashion inconsistencies in apparel. Our approach leverages Transformer architecture, incorporated with Fashion-oriented contrastive pre-training and Fashion-aware fine-tuning. Contrasting images of differing styles enhances our model's ability to recognize inconsistencies, while fine-tuning using fashion rules incorporates expert knowledge. As a result, our model excels in ingestion-based and query-based inconsistency detection benchmarks, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin.

This overview introduces several advanced theories of non-classical electromagnetic fields, focusing particularly on generalized statistical ensembles. By applying traditional quantum theory and theorems such as Schrödinger's and Heisenberg's uncertainty principles, we explore multiple applications of these modern frameworks. Additionally, we introduce a new method for testing the classical nature of light based on joint measurements of orthogonal field components and their products. Our experimental results demonstrate that light in a thermal state fails such a classicality test. The outcome of our work provides impetus for further investigations using advanced quantum states of light and novel theory-proposal approaches to quantum mechanics.

A crucial challenge in federated learning, a decentralized machine learning method, lies in synchronizing updates from diverse client devices. The standard approach employs synchronous aggregation, however, this often leads to updated parameters being aggregated before they've been sufficiently trained. In this research, we investigate the scenario where the server accumishes gradients over multiple time steps before synchronizing them. Our theoretical findings confirm that this unconstrained federated approach yields superior performance over asynchronous aggregation. Furthermore, under the assumption of independent and identically distributed data, empirical results demonstrate that adaptive methods, including federated momentum, significantly outperform baseline federated training algorithms.

This study calms the joint compositions of functions of multiple variables,
specifically within the spaces $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$ by
expressing them as series expansions in terms of Hermite and Wiener polynomials.
These calculations are applicable to a broader class of functions beyond those
limited to tempered growth. This research extends the findings of prior work on
the function spaces $C(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $H(\mathbb{R}^N)$.

This investigation examines whether the enigmatic dimensions proposed in theoretical models could instead be comprised of dark matter and analyzes the possibility that the marshlands in holographic theories are comprised of the same elusive substance. It demonstrates that the dark matter fraction within the marshlands is proportional to the dark matter density of the primordial black holes. Since this ratio is preserved during evaporation, the marshlands themselves must be composed of these black holes unless the dimensionality of the marshlands is itself negligible.

Leaching processes cause brittle materials such as chalk and soap to break apart into smaller pieces that adhere to one another through surface tension, creating complex cellular patterns in chalk and similar substances. This study examines fractures within model systems composed of slippery, soap-like materials, utilizing large-scale simulations and real-time footage of chalk and soap films. Although these films resist deformation, they allow for the relatively smooth passage of fracture lines due to their tunable frictional properties. Various approaches have been investigated to initiate and control fractures, including the creation of preformed cracks and the use of underlying turbulent fluids that cause films to rupture. Despite these methods, the exact mechanisms governing fractures within soft materials remain poorly understood.

In gallium nitride (GaN), achieving high conductivity is a significant challenge due to its wide bandgap, but scientists have discovered that aligning its lattice with specific materials like ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ can enhance its conductivity by 10$^4$ times. This innovative method, leveraging the properties of group III nitrides in the II-III chalcogenide system, not only raises GaN's conductivity to levels suitable for device applications, but also enables the exploration of novel phenomena in this material system.

Achieving effective navigation through complex and changing environments like the ocean demands the ability to create detailed maps in real-time and make route planning decisions. Map-making is particularly challenging due to large, slow data sets and ever-varying tide conditions that impact depth measurements. To overcome these difficulties, this research proposes a novel two-stage method utilizing machine learning. The first stage creates a compact key point map from raw data using a clustering technique and develops predictive models to capture key feature variations. The second stage employs this informed map to generate a high-density, up-to-date environment model via optimal planning paths along key points. The proposed method was rigorously tested in a marine robot using real and simulated sonar data, and it demonstrated the ability to adapt to varying tide conditions and generate accurate depth estimates. The results show that our method outperforms existing approaches, such as kernel regression and nearest neighbor models.

We demonstrate how to create isometric transformations known as Darboux and Calapso transformations from meromorphically isothermal surfaces. We also establish a relationship between the two transformations, showing that they hinge on the solution of a linear differential equation. This approach enables us to explore the connections and effects of both transformations in detail.

Nonparametric regression offers greater flexibility than parametric regression but lacks structured assumptions. The main challenge in nonparametric estimation is selecting an appropriate method and evaluating its effectiveness. This chapter delves into various nonparametric estimation methods, emphasizing their theoretical underpinnings, practical implications for computing and bandwidth selection, and empirical evidence supporting their efficacy. The focus is on regression analyses utilizing cross-sectional independent and identically distributed panel data. The covered techniques encompass kernel regression, series expansions such as polynomials and splines, and quantile expectations. The chapter's computational aspects and testing procedures for model fit and specification are also discussed.

The $\lambda$r-stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted as $S_r(n,k)$, are defined by the identity $\frac{1}{t e^{\lambda t}-t}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} (-1)^m S_r(\lambda,n,m)\frac{t^m}{n!}$. We demonstrate several identities involving these numbers.

Predicting future events based on past events in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) is an area of interest. Most existing research addresses this challenge by developing model architectures that determine relationships based on multiple factors, including entity properties, relationship types, and temporal information. These models require trial and error to optimize performance, which can be time-consuming and complex. In contrast, this research explores the use of fixed model architectures for event linkage in TKGs. Although these models have a limited capacity to adapt to the characteristics of the specific dataset, their simplicity and efficiency make them worthwhile to investigate. A key contribution of this research is the development of four distinct connection prediction models for TKGs - two of which are extensions of established event relationship models and two are based on traditional recommendation systems. By leveraging information from the entire dataset, these models achieve superior performance compared to their counterparts. Furthermore, the FRCNN model outperforms five other leading approaches on two real-world datasets, showcasing the potential of these fixed model architectures.

To establish that two infinite matrices with non-negative integer entries are shift equivalent, traditional methods often rely on infinite matrices or block matrices with non-negative integer entries. However, novel criteria for robust shift equivalence for finite matrices have been proposed, which do not necessitate the use of infinite matrices. This research examines whether these new criteria ensure robust shift equivalence for finite matrices with non-negative integer entries. Furthermore, this work explores how these new criteria apply to the equivalence of directed graphs with finite arrows and their associated C*-algebras.

We have investigated how heavy quarks interact within a strongly magnetized quark-gluon plasma using the real-time path integral approach, focusing on the impact of the large magnetic field on their behavior. The large magnetic field causes the propagator of transverse variables to be suppressed, effectively confining heavy quarks to move primarily along field lines and significantly altering their interactions. Analyzing the heavy quark potential at various distances reveals an anisotropic quark-matter interaction influenced by both the large magnetic field and plasma conditions. Notably, at short distances, quarkantiquark pairs exhibit a tendency to align perpendicularly to the magnetic field, while their arrangement becomes more parallel to the field at larger separations. The anisotropic interaction gives rise to distinct melting patterns of quarkonium states, influencing their mass ratios.

Inquiring answers encompass two distinct categories: yes-no responses and explanation-based responses. Knowing a knowledge graph's logical rules enables precise model predictions of answering styles in various contexts. We utilize knowledge graph inference to improve language models capable of providing inquiring answers. By training the model using logical inference, we increase its linguistic flexibility and reduce the need for extensive explanation data. Experimental results reveal that our model surpasses previous alternatives in inquiry answering and exhibits greater robustness with limited explanation datasets. Furthermore, the application of logical rules expands the range of possible answers available to the model.

We introduce two novel expansions, the high dimensional polynomial expansion and the high dimensional Hall-Polya expansion, which serve as generalizations of well-known expansions in higher dimensions. These expansions find wide applicability in various fields such as theoretical computer science, combinatorics, and machine learning. Their rigorous establishment employs powerful techniques including covering arguments and low degree sum of squares arguments.

This research investigates the effectiveness of natural language prompts in guiding model-based selectors to identify relevant instances during the training process. We analyzed how prompt variations impact selector performance across multiple tasks, utilizing two distinct selector types and three different evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we examined the influence of prompt wording, content, length, and complexity on selector effectiveness. Notably, our results indicate that shorter prompts without explicit content reveal prompt are often more effective for tree-structured models, whereas linear models benefit from explicit descriptions in these prompts. We also explored the relationship between prompt characteristics and selector performance, investigating whether prominent selection metrics influence effectiveness. Overall, our study contributes to the field by providing actionable insights for practitioners to optimize prompt design for improved selector performance.

We define the L-invariants of Artin modules as a generalisation along the lines of Colmez and Schneider, in conjunction with their associated periods. This is achieved by analysing the L-invariants of the fundamental graded one-dimensional Artin modules. Furthermore, by examining Deligne's L-invariants for variations of Hodge structure and leveraging the L-invariants of finite order Artin representations from Darmon and Rotger, the L-invariants for general Artin modules can be understood in terms of the L-invariants of these basic, graded modules.

We've developed a Rydberg multifrequency Rybergwire microwave detection system, which leverages a Rybergatom's enhanced dipole moment by applying microwave radiation to amplify its response at neighboring frequencies. This setup detects microwaves across a broad frequency range using a simple method, but currently suffers from a limited signal-to-noise ratio due to inherent Rybergatom fluctuations. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio without extending detection time, we developed a machine learning-based classification system using a convolutional neural network. This approach effectively distinguishes between noise and true signal, yielding detection thresholds comparable to those achieved through prolonged measurement periods.

The ultra-dense dwarf galaxy UGC 8838 is a rare and unique system that features a strikingly uniform and stable disk, and when paired with a unique and elusive object, it offers an ideal platform for in-depth investigation of ancient systems. Using advanced data from multiple sources, including high-precision data from a recent study, it is possible to create an updated model of the system, and this model indicates that the system's unique properties are consistent with a much older age of around 13.8 billion years. Utilizing detailed data from a study of the system, it is possible to create an accurate model of the matter distribution in the system, and this model indicates that the mass of the paired object is around 2.0 billion times that of our planet, and is located around around around 1.6 kiloparsecs from our solar system, and is moving at a speed of around around around around around 100 km/s.

This dissertation investigates aspects of quasiregular self-mappings within a quasicontinuous framework.  We establish conditions under which the Hausdorff measure is exact on certain fractal sets and demonstrate that the Hausdorff measure behaves similarly to it on the attractor of a hyperbolic quasiregular mapping. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which the Hausdorff measure becomes null or exhaustive on such attractors. Lastly, under a specific analytic condition, we show that the set where a quasisymmetric function exhibits locally bounded behavior has full Hausdorff measure on the positive real line.

The transmission of gravity waves from the lower to the lower thermosphere on Mars remains poorly understood, primarily due to the lack of comprehensive observations of the neutral atmosphere. Recent studies have made significant advancements in the lower and lower thermospheric range by utilizing MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN density data spanning from 2004 to 2018. Our research employs a new diagnostic approach based on the vertical wavenumber of gravity waves in the thermosphere on Mars. We identified the primary source areas of gravity waves at the surface and their transmission patterns, primarily from the polar caps in the cold season and the mid-latitudes in the warm season. Notably, a 0.015/km wavenumber gravity wave was detected in the 75-85 degree latitude range with an amplitude of 1.2 km in the 2018 warm season. The findings indicate that gravity waves primarily originate from the surface and are not significantly amplified as they travel upward in the thermosphere on Mars.

A comprehensive examination of the ALICE detector's findings from 2016 to 2018 reveals evidence of forward J/psi production in Pb-Pb ultra-peripheral collisions at a $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. Utilizing two independent triggers and specific reconstruction techniques, our study investigates the characteristics of both photon-glucoun and photon-photon interactions in Pb-Pbe collisions. For gluon-denton pairs, our data are compared with simulations based on QCD calculations using Pythia 8 and PhoMe, showing that our results align with theoretical predictions for gluon-denton generation across most Pb-Pbe centrality intervals, except in the most central collisions where photon-photon pairs account for a considerable portion of our measurements. Similarly, our data are consistent with PhoMe predictions for photon-photon pairs using ALICE and ATLAS measurements of exclusive $\phi$ production to analyze the effects of breakup criteria.

A well-crafted soundtrack significantly enhances the overall experience of a movie. In line with industry standards, our approach involves creating sounds based on visual content. Unlike basic visually-driven audio production, our method gives creators more control to make decisions that contribute to the narrative. Achieving this level of sophistication requires sounds to be not just visually, but also contextually, emotionally, and stylistically relevant. To streamline this complex audio creation process, we introduce a fully automated but customizable audio creation system. This system leverages both human expertise and cutting-edge technology to identify and extract unique sound effects from movie footage that are relevant to users' custom demands through image, text, and sound features.

The application of recurrent neural networks to various problems involving temporal sequences has seen significant success in fields such as speech recognition, machine translation, and gesture recognition. This tutorial delves into the fundamental concepts and advancements of recurrent neural networks, covering theoretical and practical aspects, including smoothing, hidden state formulation, learning techniques, variance reduction, unsupervised pre-training, and more. Additionally, the inherent limitations of recurrent networks will be explored along with potential solutions to overcome these challenges.

To effectively combat epidemics, precise modeling and prediction of optimal optimal timing for intervention are required.  A universal approach to identifying precise optimal intervention times has been developed, which enables the establishment of optimal quarantine periods that minimize infection rates and economic disruption while ensuring efficient recovery periods.  Simulation and real-world data from the SARS outbreak demonstrate that implementing these precise intervention times results in significantly lower final infection rates and economic loss compared to non-adaptive strategies.  The proposed approach enables the development of optimal epidemic management policies that balance public health and economic considerations.

End-to-end machine learning workflows have become increasingly intricate, and as a result, troubleshooting data quality issues over such complex pipelines has become a significant challenge, particularly in industries outside of tech. Current approaches to data quality assessment and model performance analysis often focus on individual models or quality metrics in isolation but fail to consider machine learning workflows as a whole and the various data quality issues that arise within them. To address this gap, we introduce Shapley Significance, a method grounded in Shapley values that enables the identification of data subsets influencing model performance and data quality metrics on specific machine learning workflow components. Through extensive simulations and case studies involving three real-world datasets, we demonstrate that Shapley Significance effectively pinpointes data subsets contributing model performance degradation and data quality degradation across different machine learning pipeline parts, even in data subsets that appear to be well-labeled and clean.

This paper begins by presenting basic concepts in algebraic geometry, then focuses on the relationship between statistics and combinatorics, as well as topology, on one hand, and the application of these fields to algebraic geometry on the other.  Furthermore, it also discusses how these fields converge in the area of combinatorial and statistical algebraic geometry.

Investigating how magnetic interactions influence electronic properties in materials, particularly those with unusual arrangements of atoms like triangular lattices, reveals fascinating phenomena such as anomalous Hall effects. A recent study conducted under high pressure utilized Hall effect and neutron diffraction measurements on Mn$_3$Sn to explore the relationship between macroscopic electronic behavior and the materials' magnetic configurations. The research demonstrated a substantial decrease in both the anomalous Hall resistivity and neutron intensity as high pressure was applied, indicating a transition from ferromagnetic states to a high-pressure antiferromagnetic state with a long-range magnetic order. Notably, the transition exhibited signs of cooperativity, suggesting a symbiotic relationship between the magnetic and electronic properties. The findings can be attributed to the interplay between anomalous Hall effects and electronic correlations in triangular antiferromagnets, offering valuable insights for the design of new multiferroic materials that could potentially combine exceptional magnetoelectric characteristics.

Relation extraction involves identifying and labeling the connections between entities mentioned in texts. Traditional methods used text features and hand-crafted rules, but achieved limited success due to their high dependency on specific datasets. Recent advancements in deep neural networks have enabled more automated and robust relation extraction by learning both text features and relevant structures. This paper serves as a comprehensive guide to deep neural network-based relation extraction methods, covering feature propagation, architectural choices, and effectiveness of various techniques through extensive testing on multiple datasets for the most prevalent relation types in texts.

This paper delves into a unique boundary value problem that combines Steklov and Robin conditions, specifically how many distinct eigenvalues exist below a specified threshold within C^2 functions over a given domain. The research provides a comprehensive answer to this question under the condition of monotone boundary conditions, with further results obtained under more general conditions. The study also examines the relationship between this problem and others, such as Gabrielov's geometric approach and connections to quantum mechanics.

Traditional image restoration techniques are limited by the simple assumption of independent and identically distributed data, which does not hold true for images corrupted with salt-and-pepper noise. To overcome this shortcoming, we utilize a hypergraph to model local pixel interactions in images, allowing us to develop the Guided Hypergraph Restoration model. This innovative approach employs hyperedges with three vertices representing two adjacent pixels and one label, enabling the capture of long-range dependencies within the image. By leveraging these connections, we transform the restoration problem into a balanced labeling task, facilitating simultaneous consideration of the image's local structure and global coherence. The model can be efficiently solved using the gradient projection method, demonstrating significant improvements over previous image restoration techniques.

This study presents CX-CT, a dataset consisting of 1,000 chest X-ray images paired with corresponding computed tomography projections. CX-CT features detailed annotations including pathologies, organs, and skeletal structures, enabling task-specific data selection. The projective nature of CT images aligns well with the principles behind interpreting chest X-rays, making CX-CT an ideal tool for developing and training radiological AI models and enhancing their interpretability. A baseline CNN model was created using CX-CT to assess its effectiveness in comparison to traditionally annotated X-ray data.

We examine contact forms within hyperbolic 3-manifolds and their covers to ascertain the Thurston norm behavior of their dual curves. Specifically, we prove that the Thurston norm has a minimum of one in one-sided infinite families of hyperbolic 3-manifolds with tight contact structures. Our findings also reveal that, in any hyperbolic 3-manifold, the Euler characteristics of dual curves reach their lowest absolute values among all closed 3-manifolds. This property holds universally for dual curves in their respective hyperbolic 3-manifolds and total spaces of negative definite blow-ups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dual curves of contact structures in these manifolds maintain minimal Euler characteristics. Our research expands on typical behaviors observed in rational tressored and Seifert fibered manifolds.

We introduce a statistical physics approach based on entropy production to investigate directional emission in quantum dot microcavity lasers with and without DWELL layers. Our analysis compares the entire probability distribution of photon emission angles, revealing an overwhelmingly dominant, highly entropic flow in lasers lacking DWELL layers, characterized by minimal forward directionality. Conversely, directional emission in lasers incorporating DWELL layers exhibits lower entropy production but pronounced forward directionality, illustrating the trade-off between entropy and directed flow. These findings quantify the cost of achieving low-threshold directional emission and may guide future research in optimizing entropy consumption for efficient laser design.

This paper proposes cost consistency as a new metric for evaluating the reliability of cryptocurrency as a medium of exchange, and investigates its dynamics over time. The cost consistency of cryptocurrency as a payment method is compared to its market value. The analysis focuses on three major cryptocurrencies: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, examining their transaction costs and market prices across various exchanges. Results indicate fluctuating cost consistency patterns for each cryptocurrency, with significant variations between them. Notably, Ethereum exhibits higher cost consistency than Bitcoin and Ripple, with transaction costs remaining relatively stable as a percentage of market price, particularly from June 2017 onwards.

The widely-held theory that the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation produces anomalous scaling statistics is being questioned in favor of a conventional noise theory. The unusual and conventional theories rely on different properties of the distribution function. We show that characteristics of the distribution predicted by the unusual theory are inconsistent with the cardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. In contrast, the conventional theory is supported by statistical solutions of the cardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. Additionally, the characteristics of the distribution are being studied through high-precision simulations of the cardar-Parisi-Zhang equation.

Type I compressive turbulence, commonly found in the solar wind, is analyzed at sub-ion scales using Magnetic and Plasma data from the MMS spacecraft. The frequency-power spectra of this analysis reveal distinct characteristics: magnetic fields and cross-fields exhibit balanced, cascade-like spectra with different indices between -2.84 and -5.61; whereas parallel components show weaker power-law indices within a 5/3 range. The observed spectral indices suggest significant nonlinear effects at smaller sub-ion scales. This research additionally investigates the frequency-time turbulence characteristics using Time-Space analysis, confirming ion-scale anisotropy. The results confirm existing research findings and provide insights into smaller sub-ion scale behaviors that require further exploration.

High-intense, attosecond-duration pulses in the extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray spectrum can be generated through amplification in free-electron lasers using altered chirp-taper techniques. By optimizing these pulses' duration and carrier-envelope phase, they become suitable for conducting experiments in this region of light spectrum, enabling precise manipulation of both energy and time. The theoretical framework and computational analysis examine how key parameters affect attosecond pulse characteristics, yielding examples utilizing Next Generation X-ray FEL and Low-alpha Light Source facilities.

The researchers employed tangible optics to analyze and understand complex flow patterns within layered fluids subjected to shear stress. By leveraging the tangential component of light refraction, they could visualize and investigate these flows without disrupting their natural state. This method enabled the users to observe and study the effects of viscosity and current velocity on fluid flow patterns, particularly in systems involving movable barriers and varying viscosities. The team used this estimation method to analyze the behavior of fluids with different viscosities and to identify trends in shear current velocity based on viscosity ratios. The research demonstrated that higher viscosity fluids tend to have lower shear current velocities compared to fluids with lower viscosities. The researchers concluded that tangible optics can be an effective tool for estimating shear current velocities and investigating the properties of viscous fluids.

The challenge of detecting unfair electoral map designs has been a pressing issue in the field of politics and statistics.
This paper proposes a novel method for quantifying the degree of unfairness in electoral maps by employing concepts from Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques, specifically simulated tempering.
The proposed measure is demonstrated on real-world electoral maps for several US states, as well as a notorious partially gerrymandered US state, Indiana, in the 1990s.
The results indicate that the proposed measure is capable of accurately detecting the unfairness in Indiana's historical electoral maps, as well as providing informative insights into the levels of fairness in other US states.

The textile industry demands high-quality patterns with superior visual appeal, 
necessitating effective inspection systems that can efficiently detect flaws within 
textiles at a reasonable cost. This study presents an advanced defect 
identification method for patterned textile images, combining the template matching 
capability of the Gradient Direction Histogram and leveraging low-rank decomposition 
to enhance its performance beyond conventional approaches. This method's 
gross defect detection rate is further improved through a decision-making system 
that filters out false positives and unreliable results. Experimental outcomes 
demonstrate the proposed method's exceptional accuracy in identifying defects, 
achieving a detection rate of 99.31% and showcasing its compliance with the 
requirements of modern textile industries.

We introduce a new approach to autonomous visual navigation in complex, large-scale environments by combining deep reinforcement learning and information theory. This method uses gridworld and real-world navigation datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses existing solutions in performance, while being more efficient and finding more reliable solutions with fewer iterations. Building on this, we introduce a novel action selection technique that effectively balances exploration and exploitation, leading to improved results on benchmark tests. Finally, we provide practical guidance on hyperparameter tuning and achieve significant reduction in training time, ultimately outperforming existing methods by up to 7 times.

In the context of Hawking radiation and black hole formation, we investigate how mass changes due to the competition between the two processes. Specifically, we establish a critical threshold that dictates the minimum mass reduction rate below which black holes can form and evaporate simultaneously within the same spacetime region, assuming they stay approximately spherical. Notably, this mass reduction rate is directly proportional to the Hawking temperature of the black hole, and at room temperature, this rate is around the mass of an atomic electron.

Deep within dense galactic centers lie compact clusters of short-lived massive stars known as Population III stars. Although these Initial Mass Function stars haven't been directly detected yet, there's mounting evidence from theoretical models and observations that they may have influenced the development of their host galaxies. Specifically, these Population III stars could have contributed significantly to the formation of massive black holes, particularly in isolated environments. In contrast, within nuclear star clusters, the collapse of these stars often occurs in close proximity, leading to the formation of binary systems that emit detectable gravitational waves. Even a small fraction of Population III stars in an NC can produce a substantial gravitational-wave signal characterized by a specific amplitude and frequency, ultimately resulting in distinct observable patterns. Due to the uncertainty in the formation of these black holes, there are multiple scenarios that could unfold, prompting the need to explore the implications of these different outcomes on the detection of gravitational waves. Ultimately, the detection or non-detection of gravitational waves from sources originating in NCs can serve as a valuable tool in refining our understanding of the characteristics of these elusive Population III stars.

To address the limited availability of telemetry points in distribution networks, this research proposes a novel data-driven method for pinpointing critical events like short-circuits and reduced load. The proposed approach relies on local data from single phasor measurement units and can operate with either aggregated customer data or total load data per feeder. By comparing observed data to a learned representation of normal conditions, the method identifies anomalous events and calculates an anomaly score to distinguish significant events from routine fluctuations. Experiments conducted on a realistic feeder network demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in detecting various fault types and parameter reductions.

The underlying nature of the X(3872) enigmatic state is investigated by examining its radiative and electroweak decay processes, including $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$, $X(3872)\rightarrow D^0 \bar{D}^{*0}$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow D^* \bar{D^*0}$. Within the framework of dispersion relations and assuming the X(3872) as a molecular state, theoretical estimates are formulated, notably the partial widths for X(3872) decays, which are compared with available experimental data, and also real parts of transition amplitudes, which can be tested via the Bloch equations. Our calculations for decay widths are in agreement with experimental findings, and we compute the real part of the transition amplitude with estimated error margins, also considering isospin-violating decay processes as evidence for the molecular nature of X(3872).

We define specific categories, $YDQ(X)$, associated with a smooth projective variety $X$, encompassing quadratic forms on vector bundles over $X$. By analyzing the characteristics and relations within these categories through exact sequences and vector bundle morphisms, we identify and establish quadrics within them. Furthermore, determining the symmetric S2-equivalence class of a quadratic form on a vector bundle corresponds directly with classifying the associated quadric according to Iskovskikh's methodology. Subsequently, symmetric S2-equivalence classes of such quadratic forms represent distinct geometric objects – rational forms of the underlying vector bundle's associated projective space, in which the associated quadric represents a distinct rational form of the corresponding projective space.

Text-based games provide a direct interface to understand fundamental concepts in grammar and reasoning by modeling relationships between texts. Our new text-based game platform, TextWorldExpress, enables large-scale simulations by providing a high-speed simulation speed of over one million actions per second, enhancing its previous version's simulation speed of approximately 3,000 actions per second. Moreover, TextWorldExpress supports both basic and advanced rules for parsing text actions, resulting in a significant improvement in the emulation of text-based games and reinforcement learning performance for models like transformers, feedforward networks, and tree models.

To model and comprehend phenomena arising in genuine topological insulators, we need to develop effective methods for Topological Insulators formed through geometric topological mechanisms. By building upon our previous works where we created artificial topological insulators and discovered robust edge states even in systems lacking a band gap, we now propose an "A-geometric method" to generate robust edge states in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional Topological Insulators exhibiting disorder. Our approach enables us to establish a reliable geometric topological invariant that remains unaffected by various types of disorder. Moreover, we can control the position of the edge states by fine-tuning system parameters, thus demonstrating the feasibility of our method in scenarios involving disorder.

Harnack-type inequalities are established for $p$-harmonic functions within specific two-dimensional sectors, particularly when the angular width of the sectors meets certain criteria. These inequalities are initially derived for the extreme cases of $p$ values ($p<2$ and $p>2$) through an approach that utilizes the minimum and maximum principles in the context of these two dimensional sectors. This methodology enables the extension of $C^{0,\alpha}$-Harnack inequalities to $p$-subharmonic and $p$-superharmonic functions in two-dimensional cones, particularly when the angular width satisfies specific constraints and the angle variations satisfy Laplacian comparisons. Additionally, this logic facilitates the examination of Harnack-type inequalities in higher-dimensional cones and cones with smooth boundaries.

Using a well-known multivariate extreme value model, researchers have developed a novel approach to modeling extreme values in various dimensions while considering the influence of external covariates. The method is demonstrated using real-world data from an infamous storm in Europe and additional datasets related to sand duster events in Australia. The analysis reveals that taking covariate effects into consideration substantially enhances the accuracy of modeling extreme wind speeds in certain directions. The research also highlights that this improved accuracy translates to more reliable predictions of environments necessary for safe aircraft landings during such storms.

Let $k$ be a fixed algebraic closure of a finite field, and let $A$ be an arbitrary fixed abelian variety defined over $k$. We establish that only a limited number of non-constant functions with coefficients in $k$ non-constant over the canonical place of $k$ can be mapped to points on $A$ that are not $k$-linearly dependent on the identity map of $A$. Similarly, we confirm Mordell-Lang's conjecture as demonstrated by Hindry and Silverman, which states that a similar limitation applies when considering the projected image in $\mathbb{P}^n_k$ of these functions where $x_0$ in each function is constant.

A recently proposed method called human-realm adjustment enables a robot to take over task execution from a human operator when they encounter difficulties. The operator provides input through unpredictable force impulses while the robot determines required effort using a pre-set manipulability threshold. However, achieving precise threshold settings remains challenging due to differences in task complexity and underlying dynamics. This issue is particularly pronounced when the robot is mounted on a conveyor system that moves parallel to both human and robot motion, altering the robot's dynamics and necessitating frequent recalibration of the threshold. In this research, we present an improved approach that allows the robot to adapt its manipulability threshold in real-time without requiring prior knowledge of the task or extensive parameter estimation. Furthermore, we propose using an advanced icp-based pose estimation method compatible with the force-based interaction to improve the robot's end-effector position accuracy and thereby enhance the effectiveness of the human-realm adjustment approach. Experimental results are provided to validate the proposed solution.

A key component of the Standard Model, the Higgs boson pair creation process offers significant insights into its own properties and the underlying parameters. Due to the extremely rare occurrence of this process, experimental detection at current collider facilities is beyond reach. Its potential is best fulfilled with future colliders such as the CLIC or ILC. Investigating this process in the specific final state $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ with a precision of 5% using the matrix element technique provides crucial information. Specifically, this analysis examines the differential cross-sections and different spin configurations of intermediate Higgs bosons in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.

Our approach employs unsupervised learning to teach agents to understand the 3D positioning of objects in their environment by detecting and analyzing unintentional rotations of objects caused by camera movement. By using everyday objects that rotate in the scene, agents can learn a fundamental concept of 3D space effectively. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that agents trained with this method can successfully navigate through scenes containing rotating objects at various speeds and speeds of UNINTENTIONAL ROTATIONS.

A persistent challenge in combating COVID-19 misinformation is the task of accurately identifying users' ultimate stance on the misinformation. Our study targets this challenge by introducing MeVaxUltra, a sophisticated Twitter dialogue model named MeVaxUltra that can accurately determine users' acceptance or refusal of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. Building on the existing MeVax model, which excels in determining users' acceptance or refusal of misinformation posts in isolation, MeVaxUltra extends its capabilities to analyze entire Twitter dialogues. This advancement acknowledges the critical role user interactions play in the spread of misinformation. Empirical testing demonstrates that MeVaxUltra significantly outperforms its predecessor and several competing baseline models, achieving a F1-score of 0.8533.

To explore the response of matter to extremely brief field spikes, specifically those lasting less than 100 attoseconds, we propose a method using attosecond electron pulses in a tunneling gas mirror. When a strong field spike interacts with these pulses, it induces a coherent burst of high-harmonic emission, consisting of few-carrier wavepackets generated within approximately 40 attoseconds. This process can be sequestered from surrounding spontaneous emission by finely-tuning the overlap of the pulses, and enables the creation of isolated attosecond charge currents switchable on a sub-cycle basis.

We generated synthetic light curves for 20 potential companion stars in the Algol system by applying standardized photometric models. Analyzing actual light curve observations, we determined that eight of these candidates exhibit distinct eclipsing patterns consistent with similar stars elsewhere in the Algol system. Notably, stars HD 153373 and HD 196253 show fresh evidence of new companions, likely due to previously undetected blue main sequence stars. Our findings suggest that the Algol system may be expanding and that fresh contenders may emerge in the near future.

We investigate explosion solutions to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a positive absorption term outside the geometric shape of a convex mirror's reflecting surface. By employing Pohozaev-type identities, we demonstrate that explosion solutions exist for $L^2$-bounded problems when the initial data resides within a specific region in an infinite Hilbert space. Our analysis also reveals that as the initial data approaches the boundary of this region in the Hilbert space, the $L^2$ norm of the solution converges to that of the free Schrödinger equation's explosion solution.

Physically-informed neural networks utilize gradient-based optimization to solve partial differential equations, integrating physical laws like conservation and equilibrium principles into the network's objective function. Building upon this concept, we introduce Residual-Driven Adaptive Node Generation, a ResNet-based node creation framework that enhances PINNs by dynamically introducing new nodes in regions with significant error. By resolving finer-scale problems with these new nodes, the network can concentrate on learning the residual error and converge more efficiently. Our method outperforms standard adaptive refinement techniques and traditional solution methods by accelerating training and improving error without the need for additional hyperparameters. Furthermore, the framework generalizes well and displays robust numerical stability even with very small errors.

The combination of negative capacitance (NC) and domain wall (DW) logic presents itself as a promising technology, which leverages the energy from clock pulses to manipulate ferroelectric domains and generate additional bits per material. A novel field effect transistor (FeFET) structure has been developed that utilizes a single clocking pulse per bit to manipulate a domain wall (DW) logic. By integrating a spin transfer torque (STT) effect, we can achieve bit erasure, which was previously unattainable solely through the use of an electrostatic force. Our research involved creating a multi-dimensional NC-FEFeFET simulation, which incorporates aspects of electronics and magnetism, utilizing advanced models. These simulations enabled the examination of the behaviors of the device under various conditions, including the effects of capacitance, magnetic anisotropy, and more, which were validated against experimental data. Our results indicate that the proposed DW-FeFET can store two informational bits in a single physical element, which becomes three bits when the external clocking signal is considered as an additional bit, offering significant improvements in storage density and energy efficiency.

To effectively manage the U.S. freight transportation network, the U.S. Department of Transportation seeks a comprehensive understanding of its underlying dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. In an effort to address this understanding, the Research and Advanced Technology Evaluator for Freight (RAT-E-Freight) developed the Freight Ecosystem Dependency-Fragility Insight Graph (FEDFI-G), which models the interconnected relationships between freight components and their respective transportation modes. By utilizing FEDFI-G, RAT-E-Freight conducted user-driven simulations to assess the extent to which disruptions propagate through the freight system when specific nodes or connections are compromised. By leveraging the graph's theoretical framework and properties, they were able to develop an efficient user-driven model for analyzing fragility dissemination within the freight network.

This study delves into the ergodic properties of an intricate Ginzburg-Landau equation subject to stochastic perturbations modeled by Poisson random measures. Initially, the theoretical mathematical framework for these equations, taking into consideration pure jump disturbances, is established. Subsequently, under specific conditions ensuring the irreducibility of the associated Markov process, sufficient criteria for ergodicity are derived via a sufficient criteria for irreducibility. Notably, the theoretical findings are supported and validated through numerical simulations, illustrating the practical significance of the developed mathematical theories.

Let G be a finite group. We establish a precise relationship between the maximal power degree in the non-edge set of G's Cayley digraph and G being a specific type of abelian group. Additionally, if G is a nilpotent group, we determine both the minimum and maximum possible values for the power degree in the non-edge set of G's Cayley digraph.

A high-precision detector system known as ASACUS is meticulously built into the CERNLEAR3 beamline at Geneva to study the properties of neutral particles such as photons, neutrons, and electronic neutrinos. By doing so, the instrument contributes significantly to advanced research areas, including the investigation of nuclear reactions, searches for rare events and beyond-standard-model physics, as well as the study of cosmic radiation phenomena. This work presents an in-depth analysis of the intricate ASACUS experiment apparatus and its underlying theoretical framework, offering additional insights into the study of unusual decays and parity-violating elastic scattering.

This study explores the performance of orientation-sensitive building blocks 
within the context of image recognition tasks, building on the novel concept 
first presented at the International Conference on Image Processing in 2019.

Geometric features in point clouds are essential for various real-world applications. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) serve as the foundation for numerous point cloud processing tasks but their performance can be hindered by traditional approaches that convert neighborhoods into input matrices. A new framework called Attention-based Graph Convolutional Networks (AGCN) is proposed to overcome this limitation. By employing an attention mechanism, AGCN dynamically identifies and extracts neighborhoods based on the network's current state, in contrast to traditional GCNs which use static methods. This new approach is shown to yield improved results over existing GCNs. Furthermore, AGCN addresses the issue of sub-optimal backpropagation during training by introducing the concept of dynamic subgraphs. This allows only forward and backward computations involving neighborhood point selections, reducing computational complexity and data propagation errors. The performance benefits of AGCN are validated through evaluations on multiple datasets and the framework's versatility is demonstrated in multiple real-world applications.

Recent studies have uncovered specific hostless Trojans designed to deceive detection by employing deceptive and benign-appearing code segments that conceal malicious code through control flow transfer techniques. However, this method becomes vulnerable when attempts are made to analyze and deceive the Trojan, as any such effort often exposes the malicious code. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a new hostless Trojan technique, which utilizes meaningful hostless trojan artifacts to maintain its integrity without becoming activatable. The proposed SemHostLioTrojan can present itself with legitimate-looking dynamic semHostLioTrojan artifacts, masking its true nature and preventing activation. This method can circumvent hostless Trojans' inherent limitations, as it allows SemHostLioTrojan to present itself with meaningful semHostLioTrojan artifacts, thereby avoiding detection even when users attempt to analyze it. Effective identification of SemHostLioTrojan requires a deep comprehension of the program's functional operations, which this paper argues can be achieved through the utilization of dynamic analysis.

We introduce an update on the ROSIE Integral Field Device currently being used on the Magellan IMACS spectrometer, emphasizing its advancement in the integration of a new cross-dispersion grating to eliminate the need for spatial binning and enhance spectral resolution to as much as 3000. This setup allows for spectral ranges between 4000-9000 Angstroms and 4000-6500 Angstroms using respective broad and narrow band filters, along details on its design, testing procedures, current performance metrics, upcoming developments and data reduction methods are presented.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion reaction is revisited, focusing on the analysis of experimental data and various theoretical models to explore the concept of intrinsically repulsive potential. Further aspects of C + C fusion related to astrophysical jams, stochastic resonant tunneling, and C + O reactions are discussed, concluding with an promotion of the Trojan horse technique in addressing a potential crisis within astrophysical applications of this reaction.

Knowing the chemical makeup of a star that hosts an exoplanet is essential for predicting the terrestrial planet's internal structure and composition, especially its core mass size. This information will help refine core mass estimates via chemo-dynamical modeling. The relationship between a star's heavy element abundance (denoted as [M/H]) and its overall mass is a fundamental area of study in astrophysics. [M/H] influences both a star's opacity and the efficiency of convection within its interior. The relationship between [M/H] and core mass must be taken into account when estimating the mass within an exoplanet's core. This study utilized data from the first two papers in a series to analyze the compositions of 53 planets similar in size to Earth. The results indicate that core mass can range from 10% to 70% of an exoplanet's total mass. Core mass tends to increase as the mass of its host star increases beyond 1.05 solar masses. The maximum core mass fraction for three Earth-sized planets is about 40%, which is close to the mass within Jupiter's core. The core mass fraction for super-Earths can exceed these maximum values. These findings will enhance our ability to model core masses accurately, taking the influence of host star mass into account and thus improving our capacity to constrain core masses.

Our proposal focuses on subcarrier CSI wireless positioning, where the transmitting antenna and subcarriers are seen as separate channels and pooled together to form a single high-dimensional distribution representing the user's location. To overcome the low information content of each subcarrier, we propose leveraging attention mechanisms that enable each subcarrier to prioritize relevant channel characteristics from others, thereby enhancing the overall understanding of the location. Experimented results show that the proposed approach yields substantial improvements in positioning accuracy over conventional methods.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for the semantic interpretation of basic modal logic within topological spaces, where the modality $\Diamond\phi$ is defined as "there exists a locally accessible world where $\phi$ holds." This new interpretation departs from the traditional set-theoretic approach by retaining existence and universal quantification as in the first-order logic but reinterpreting existence quantification and modality through the lens of modality and connectivity respectively, both inherent to topological spaces. By REplacing the standard logical operations with topological equivalents such as closure for disclusion and interior for extension, this new framework replaces the standard logical operations with topological equivalents, where closure and interior respectively. By Recasting the logical operations through topological properties, existence quantification and modality through the concepts of accessibility and connectivity respectively, this new framework provides new insights into the relationship between logic and topology.

Bopor and Zamfirescu discovered that almost all cubic bipartite graphs can have their edges colored red and blue such that all red edges appear on the perimeter of any drawn representation. To build upon this finding, we examine the subset of 3-connected cubic bipartite graphs and identify a large proportion (over 99.9%) that meet Bopor and Zamfirescu's criteria. However, we find a specific type of cubic bipartite graph (a Yost graph) that does not meet this edge-coloring standard, representing less than 0.01% of the total. Despite being rarely met, we prove that a modified version of this graph always can have its edges colored according to the required standard.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of an $n$-dimensional Hamming graph, where these functions are eigenfunctions of the graph, belonging to a specific set of indices $\Lambda$, with the Hamming distance denoted by $d_\mathrm{H}$. Our focus is on determining the minimum possible support size for such functions, where the support is understood as the smallest number of points necessary to accurately represent the function. For instances where the dimension $n$ is two or greater, with non-trivial indices $\Lambda$ containing more than the maximum degree $m-1$, or with one element and where it is less than $m-1$, with $m$ being one plus the first prime number that can be expressed as the sum of two squares, we determine that the minimum support is given by $2^{d_\mathrm{H}(z)}$, with the point $z$ that achieves this minimum support, with the support being unique, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being invariant under permutations, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero, with the support being functionally dependent on $f$ being non-zero

COPASI, a widely-used computational tool for analyzing biochemical systems, offers a comprehensive environment for model building, simulation, and parameter estimation through its user-friendly interface. However, accessing COPASI's powerful capabilities via its programming API can be cumbersome, especially for users seeking to integrate it into custom applications or services. To bridge this gap, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based interface that enables users to remotely operate COPASI models through a convenient web UI. By leveraging the Shiny framework, this tool allows for seamless integration of uploaded COPASI models, parameter variation, and real-time data visualization, all accessible via a web browser. Its ability to facilitate remote interaction makes ShinyCPIasi particularly valuable for cloud-based computing and future developments in cloud-based collaborative modeling environments.

One of the significant hurdles in developing reliable AI for medical imaging is ensuring that interpretations are both consistent and trustworthy. To achieve this, we need to establish a clear framework for measuring ambiguity in medical imaging, incorporating assessments of uncertainty and bias. To contribute to this endeavor, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation method that enables direct comparisons of various ambiguity measurement techniques by creating a shared framework and a publicly available dataset with expert interpretations of 500 chest X-rays along with diagnostic outcomes. Our approach allows us to test and compare multiple methods, showcasing that no single technique excels across all scenarios, but we provide guidance on choosing the most suitable method based on the specific requirements and constraints of each application. By making our evaluation process and dataset accessible to others, we aim to foster healthy competition and continuous improvement in ambiguity measurement, ultimately leading to more accurate and trustworthy diagnoses in clinical settings.

We examine von Neumann algebras generated by category functions within a compact quantum group and their associated center. If the category functions generate a central von Neumann algebra, we demonstrate that it can be centrally decomposed into a direct integral of type I factors. Furthermore, if the category functions are massive, we show they produce a factor. This analysis also leads to a new proof of the center being finite for sl₂.

This strategy iteration-like method utilizes rough upper and lower value functions to create a pair of linear systems with uncertain coefficients in finite Markov decision processes. By solving this system approximately using GMRES, the proposed strategy approximate iteration computes these bounds on the value function and strategy. Conversely, another method can find the optimal policy in a way similar to policy evaluation, requiring only one linear system to be solved approximately as well.

Let $\vec{G}=(\{1,\ldots, \deg_{\vec{g}}(x)\},\mathcal{E}(\vec{g}),\vec{x})$ be a multidirected graph with multiple edges, where the outdegree of vertex $x$ is denoted by $\deg_{\vec{g}}(x)$ and $\vec{g}$ is a function assigning a generator to each vertex. The edge ideal of $\vec{G}$, denoted by $I_{\vec{G}}$, is the ideal generated by the edge products in $S=\mathbb{K}[y_1,\ldots, y_{\deg_{\vec{g}}(x)}]$. 

We determine the border stratification of the projective toric variety associated with $\vec{G}$ and its stratification types under the action of $\GL(\mathbb{K})$. Furthermore, we prove that the border dimensions of these variety types correspond to the border codimensions of the ideal types with the same sharing patterns. These results generalize findings of [DSW20] for undirected graphs and provide context for further exploration of the border stratification of directed graphs in [SSS21].

This paper tackles an inverse problem associated with computer simulations producing time series data under various parameter settings, resulting in diverse dynamics. We propose an assessment method that evaluates multiple time series on a complex plane using an algorithm based on the argument principle. This method serves as a measure of similarity for time series, captured at distinct parameter settings. We demonstrate the approach's capability to identify dynamics across a wide range of parameters with moderate time computational costs. Furthermore, our results reveal that it can successfully resolve the inverse issue by pinpointing parameters corresponding to observed data. We apply the method to the analysis of numerical solutions for the Hodgkin-Huxley and Lotka-Morale models and discuss its practical applications for exploring a wide range of parameter settings.

As autonomous learning becomes more common in robotics, there's an increasing need for methods that allow robots to learn effectively even when faced with unexpected disruptions in their environment. This paper presents a novel approach where robots can learn in multiple geographic areas, and share their knowledge with robots in other regions to adapt their policies to their local surroundings. This collaborative learning method allows each region to contribute to a shared knowledge base and promotes knowledge transfer between regions to facilitate adaptive learning. We assess the performance of this collaborative learning in comparison to centralized learning and individual learning in each region, and provide theoretical guarantees that support its use.

The reconstruction of jets in high-energy collisions is crucial for understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Jets containing a high-energy photon are particularly useful as they are minimally affected by initial interactions. This allows researchers to focus on final interactions and the energy loss experienced by the remaining parton. Our analysis examines how fragmentation changes in such jets and compares interactions with lead-gold collisions, despite having the same center-of-mass energy. Using the ALICE detector at the LHC, we observed fragmentation changes in PbAu collisions at 8.16 TeV, but not in pp collisions, which suggests that the effect is not due to high energy but is rather a result of nuclear effects.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has uncovered compelling connections between the values of colored multiple zeta expressions and Apéry-type series features. Building upon previous studies, this current work delves even deeper into these connections by deriving novel identities that relate these expressions to alternating multiple zeta values through the mechanism of term differentiation.

Recent data from the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope and Gaia mission allow for a more accurate study of the brown dwarf WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously called GJ 580E.
